An empty marking *shall* hold no token in any place.
*When* a token is added to a place, the marking *shall* append it at the tail of that place's queue and leave the queue of every other place unchanged.

*When* the first token of a marked place is removed, the marking *shall* return the head of that place's queue and keep the rest of that queue in order, leaving the queue of every other place unchanged.
*If* the first token of a place that is not marked is removed, *then* the marking *shall* return no token and change no queue.
*When* a token is added to or removed from a marking, the resulting marking *shall* still hold a queue for each place of its net.
assumes: The model is a store Ops : MarkingOps N T (glossary GlossaryQueue.lean), the one interface CORE-070 and CONC-022 are stated over. N is the place identity (glossary: Place; identity by name, CORE-002) and T the token, kept abstract: a token's value and created_at are not constrained here, only which token sits where in a queue. view reads each place's queue, so 'FIFO queue' and 'queue order' are the glossary term Queue order; Marked is the glossary term on the count view (count s p not zero).

ok s p is 'the store s holds a queue for p'. The queue marking of the reference (refQOps) holds one for every place in every state (ok is True); a store compiled for one net (the precompiled ring pool, CONC-022) holds one for each place of that net, and only while it is well formed. 'The places of its net' is read as a finite list of places P, so the first line says that every net has an empty marking that holds all of its places (for the ring pool, a pool with one ring per place id up to the largest one, CORE_070_ringStore). The three closure clauses (a place the marking held is still held after add, after a marked removal and after an unmarked removal) are the last quoted sentence, which is the third applied to the marking an operation leaves. Together with the first line they make the third quoted sentence hold of every marking reached from the empty marking of a net by the operations (CORE_070_reach), which is how 'a marking holds a queue for each place of its net' is read: a state the store never reaches from such an empty marking is not a marking of that net, and nothing is claimed of it. Without the closure clauses the operation lines constrain one step from a held state only (CORE_070_mutant_noClosure_ring and CORE_070_mutant_noClosure_map); without the first line's 'every place of P at once' a store whose states each hold one place passes (CORE_070_mutant_somePlace_killed).

The operation lines protect the places q that the state holds (ok s q), which by the reading above are the places of its net; 'every other place' in the add and removal sentences is read as every other place of the net, the places the marking holds a queue for. A place outside the net is not part of the marking and is not constrained. The precompiled ring pool shows why the premise is needed: a place id beyond the pool's place count has no ring, and the pool says nothing about what reading it would show.

The designated empty marking Ops.empty is read at the view only (the second line): it holds no token in any place. It is not required to hold a place. The glossary store refRingStore takes as Ops.empty the pool over no place (emptyPool), which holds no place (core070_ringEmpty_holds_none), because a ring pool is sized when the net is compiled; the empty marking of a net is the state the first line provides. A consequence: a store whose designated empty state holds no place and whose add from that state loses the token is accepted, since adding to a place a marking does not hold is not an operation the spec describes. Tying Ops.empty to the places of a net needs an empty marking indexed by the place list in the glossary interface (MarkingOps, shared with CONC-022), which is outside this block.

The first two quoted sentences are prose that the EARS sentences after them restate: 'the current distribution of tokens across all places' is the first line together with the count line and the closure clauses, and 'Internally, each place maps to a FIFO queue' is the view of each place and the add and removal lines. Across a sequence of operations the queue is first in, first out: from the empty marking of a net, a sequence of adds leaves at each place exactly the tokens added there, in the order added (CORE_070_adds), and a removal then returns the first of them (CORE_070_fifo). 'Internally' does not single out one storage: both the queue marking (CORE_070_reference) and the precompiled ring pool (CORE_070_ringStore) satisfy the block.

The removal lines are read at the view and at ok: removing from a place that is not marked changes no queue and no count and keeps every place held, which is what an observer of the marking can see. Whether the store's internal state is untouched is not claimed. The precompiled ring pool's own removal (ring_remove_first, precompiled_backend.rs:396-403) is a private operation with the precondition 'the place is marked': on an unmarked place it would panic on its unwrap, and its callers check the count first. Its Lean model Pool.removeFirst advances the head index there, which leaves a pool that is no longer well formed (core070_ringRaw_unmarked_breaks). The block is therefore checked against the ring pool with the removal its callers perform, guarded by the count (core070_ringMarking), which is the marking interface (Marking.remove_first in Rust, removeFirst in Java and TypeScript, all returning no token on an unmarked place).

The operations are one step each; a sequence of operations is their composition (CORE_070_reach). Which operations a firing performs, and in which order, is EXEC-010, EXEC-012, EXEC-013 and EXEC-020: a firing's deposit is one add per emitted token, in emission order (refQFire_deposit_adds). Removal of a matching token (the correlated ν input, NU-020) and removal of every token (the reset drain, CORE-034, EXEC-013) are other operations, not stated here; so is peek (EXEC-012, CONC-022), which CORE-070 does not mention.
Who may call the operations (only the orchestrator; actions never touch the live marking) is CORE-071, and the snapshot form of a marking is CORE-073; neither is encoded here.
AC1 (an empty marking has zero tokens in all places) is the first line (the empty marking of a net) and the second line (the designated empty marking).

AC2 (tokens can be added and removed from specific places) is the first line (every place of a net is held by its empty marking) together with the add line and the two removal lines, each of which changes only the place it names and keeps every place held, so any sequence of adds and removals on the places of a net is constrained at every step (CORE_070_reach).
AC3 (the token count per place is queryable) is the count line: count is the length of the place's queue, and the add and removal lines say how it moves.

The test derivation (empty marking, three tokens added to P, count 3, one removed, count 2) is a consequence of the statement for every store, from the empty marking of any net containing P (CORE_070_derivation), which also gives that the token removed is the first one added; CORE_070_nonvacuous runs it on the reference.

requirements.title: Initial Marking
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] I R Q ↦
  (∀ (X : TimedNet N) (m0 : CountMarking N) (now0 : ℕ), (I X m0 now0).m = m0) ∧
    (∀ (X : TimedNet N) (m0 : CountMarking N) (now0 : ℕ) (u : Reference.Trans N),
        InNet X u →
          Enabled u m0 →
            (I X m0 now0).stamp u.core.name = some (ClockReading (I X m0 now0))) ∧
      (∀ (X : TimedNet N) (p : N),
          UnknownPlace X p →
            (∀ (δ : ℕ),
                on fun s s' ↦ R X s (TLbl.delay δ) s', shall fun s s' ↦ s'.m p = s.m p) ∧
              (∀ (u : Reference.Trans N),
                  on fun s s' ↦ R X s (TLbl.reap u) s', shall fun s s' ↦ s'.m p = s.m p) ∧
                ∀ (t : Reference.Trans N) (d : List N),
                  on fun s s' ↦ R X s (TLbl.fire t d) s', shall fun s s' ↦
                    s.m p ≤ s'.m p) ∧
        ∀ (X : TimedNet N) (p : N),
          UnknownPlace X p →
            ∀ t ∈ X.net.transitions,
              ∀ (δ : Delivered N T) (e : List (N × T)),
                on fun M M' ↦ Q t M δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦ M p <+: M' p
reading: For every initialiser I, timed step relation R and queue firing relation Q:
for every timed net X, initial marking m0 and start reading now0, the state I X m0 now0 holds exactly m0, on every place, whether or not the net declares it;

in the state I X m0 now0, every transition of the net that m0 enables holds the state's own clock reading as its stamp (with line 1: a transition of the net is armed there exactly when m0 enables it, and its elapsed time is 0);
for an unknown place p of X, a delay of R and a reap of R leave p's token count as it is, and a firing of R leaves p with at least the tokens it had;
every firing under Q of a transition of X leaves the queue an unknown place of X had before the firing as a prefix of its queue after it: every token kept, in its order, at the head.
quotes: An executor can be initialized with an initial marking that pre-populates places with tokens before execution begins.

*When* an executor is initialized with an initial marking, its marking *shall* hold, before execution begins, exactly the tokens the initial marking puts on each place, whether or not the net declares that place.

*When* execution begins, a transition of the net *shall* be armed exactly when its enablement check passes on the initial marking, with the firing clock's reading at that moment as its stamp, so that its elapsed time starts at 0 ([TIME-010]).
*While* a place is an unknown place, the executor *shall* retain its tokens in the marking, in their order and ahead of any token that reaches the place later, and *shall not* drop any of them.
*While* a place is an unknown place, the executor *shall not* change its tokens when the firing clock advances or when it reaps a transition ([TIME-013]).
assumes: The initialiser I X m0 now0 is the state an executor starts from (glossary: Init): the marking, the reading of the firing clock and a stamp per transition name, for the timed net X, the initial marking m0 as token counts and the first clock reading now0. A step of R (glossary: TRel) is a delay of the clock, a reap or an atomic firing. A firing of Q (glossary: QFireRel) is one step Q t M δ e M' on queue markings, which carry token identity and order. Unknown place, Armed, Elapsed time and Enabled are the glossary terms.

The second quoted shall sentence speaks of the enablement check (glossary: Enablement check), read here as Enabled in the initial marking: for a transition that has no match specification the enablement check passes exactly when the transition is enabled (CONC-008, its fourth shall sentence), and the transitions of the model (Reference.Trans) carry no match specification, so every transition of the net is such a transition (ruling D30). For a transition with a match specification the check also needs a name of which every correlated input holds at least its required count of tokens (NU-020); that case is not encoded here.

Unknown place (glossary): no transition of the net has an arc on the place or names it in its output spec. A net of the model is its list of transitions and a place exists by use, so a place declared through the builder but touched by no arc (CORE-040 AC1) is an unknown place here, although AC3 speaks of 'places the net does not declare' and the runtimes warn only for a place the compiled net does not hold. Lines 3 and 4 therefore cover more places than AC3 names, never fewer, and line 1 is on every place. The places list of a Lean net plays no part in the statement; the mutant initialiser core072_dropInit uses it as the compiled place set.

Places are identified by name here, as transitions are under ruling D10: a place of the model is its name. Java identifies a place by its name and its token type together (the Place record, the divergence MOD-024 records), so in Java an initial token on a place with the net's name but another token type is on an unknown place there, retained, inert and warned about, while in TypeScript and Rust it is on the net's place and can enable a transition. Line 2 therefore arms differently across the runtimes for such a marking; the block does not encode that case, which is MOD-024's divergence, not CORE-072's.

Transitions are identified by name (ruling D10): line 2 ranges over the transitions the net holds under their own names (InNet), line 4 over the members of the transition list, and under pairwise distinct names (NamesDistinct) the two are the same set (inNet_iff_mem).

Fusion sets (MOD-060, MOD-061) are not modelled: a Lean net has no fused members. Initial tokens on a non-canonical member of a fusion set stay on that name, which the built net no longer declares, in the runtimes: the built net keeps no fusion map (the Rust core rebuilds the fused `PetriNet` from its places, transitions, subnet membership and terminals only), no executor knows a fusion set, and Java tells the caller to concentrate initial tokens on the canonical place itself (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/FusionSet.java:36-44; clash mod-c#1). Whether MOD-061 AC2 is restated to match is ruling D54 (W8); line 1 states CORE-072's own text, which the runtimes follow, and does not depend on D54.

Line 1 is the body sentence and the first quoted shall sentence, on token counts: the initial state's marking is the initial marking, as a function on every place, so an initialiser that drops the tokens of an undeclared place (core072_dropInit, the declared-only mutant) or starts from the empty marking (core072_emptyInit) violates it. The quoted sentence says 'exactly the tokens'; the timed state of Phase 1 carries counts only, so token identity and order in the initial state are not visible here. A state with queues is the executor cycle relation's (RefExec, W5), and that a restored marking keeps identity and order is CORE-073's subject (W3).

Line 2 is the second quoted shall sentence: every transition of the net that the initial marking enables holds the initial state's clock reading as its stamp. With line 1 it gives InitArms in full (core072_initArms): a transition of the net is armed in the initial state exactly when the initial marking enables it (the 'only when' half follows from line 1 alone, since Armed includes Enabled in the state's own marking), and its elapsed time is 0 (initArms_elapsed). This is the first case of TIME-010's quoted sentence on being newly armed ('A transition is newly armed when it is enabled in the initial marking'), which TIME_010.lean leaves outside its step relation. An initialiser that holds the marking but arms nothing (core072_noArmInit) violates line 2, and so does one that arms the right transitions with a stale stamp (core072_staleStampInit: the reading 0 while the clock reads now0, as a runtime that seeds its enable times from a zeroed buffer), which the arming-only mutant reading accepts; under it a Deadline(5) transition is expired before the first step (core072_staleStamp_expired) where the reference has it ready (core072_ref_ready). Line 2 does not fix the clock reading itself: elapsed times, which are all that timing reads, depend on the difference between the clock and the stamp, and the clock is TIME-010's and TIME-015's.

AC2 ('Execution begins with these tokens available') is read as line 2: the initial tokens are available to a transition when it is armed on them with elapsed time 0, so its earliest bound counts from the start of the run. No line ties I to R: lines 3 and 4 hold on every state, the initial one included, and that a run starts at I X m0 now0 and that an armed ready transition does fire are the executor cycle relation's (RefExec, W5) and the consistency witness's (Covers in ConsistencyTime.lean), not CORE-072's. The relation that never fires from the initial state is not forbidden here; CORE_072_nonvacuous shows the reference firing from it.

Line 2 does not cover a terminal place ([EXEC-042]): a run whose initial marking marks a terminal place ends before its first enablement update, so no transition is armed (rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs:385-394). The Phase 1 state has no terminal places; the exception belongs to the executor cycle relation (RefExec, W5) and is not encoded.

Lines 3 and 4 are the third and fourth quoted shall sentences, which restate the first sentence of AC3 ('retained in the observable marking (inert ...) but never silently dropped'). Line 3 is on token counts: a delay or a reap leaves an unknown place's count as it is (the fourth sentence; neither is a seam, so 'inert' means unchanged there), and a firing leaves at least the count it had. Line 4 is on queues over every firing of a transition of the net: the old queue is a prefix of the new one, so every token stays, in its order, ahead of any token added later. The timed state has no order, so the order clause of the third sentence is line 4's alone.

A firing is held to retention, not to 'unchanged' (the test derivation's word), because AC3 lets tokens reach an unknown place through the production seam, which ruling D63 (W3) settles; any deposit appends at the tail (EXEC-020), so the prefix and count lines hold under every option of D63. On the reference the unknown place is in fact unchanged on every step (core072_ref_count, core072_ref_queue), as CORE-035 lines 1 and 3 and EXEC-020 say of a place a firing does not deposit into, so a firing that adds a token to an unknown place is CORE-035's to forbid, not this block's. The injection seam is not a label of R or Q (it waits for RefExec's injection label, W5); lines 3 and 4 name the delay, reap and firing labels and so do not constrain it.

Wrong models of lines 3 and 4: a step relation whose storage keeps only the places the net lists (core072_clearR, the shape of the pre-fix precompiled pool, whose produce_token dropped a token for a place the program does not know; Libpetri.unknown_place_drop cites CORE-072 AC3) one that doubles an unknown place on every delay, as a backend that merges its side map of uncompiled-place tokens into the marking each cycle without clearing it (core072_doubleMergeR, clash conc-b#8; the retention-only mutant reading accepts it), one that rebuilds the store from the listed places on a reap (core072_clearOnReapR, the reap clause) and one that does so on a firing (core072_clearOnFireR, the firing clause) violate line 3; CORE_072_nonvacuous_delayReap shows the reference keeping the unknown place's tokens across a delay and a reap. A queue firing that rebuilds the marking from the places it touches (core072_dropQ), one that reverses an untouched queue (core072_reverseQ; the count-only mutant reading accepts it) and one that rotates it with stale copies (core072_staleRingQ, a ring whose head index moved without clearing its slots; the retention-only mutant reading accepts it) violate line 4.
AC1 (initial marking distributes tokens to specified places) is line 1 (CORE_072_nonvacuous: places 1, 2 and the unknown place 9 hold 2, 1 and 4 tokens in the initial state).

AC3 is lines 3 and 4 for its first sentence. Its second sentence, 'every backend regardless of its internal token storage', is the scope 'all executors': the Lean models are one store, and that the production backend's ring store agrees with it is CONC-022's and CONC-025's subject. Its seams are deferred as above: production into an uncompiled place through a raw output that bypasses the context waits for ruling D63 (CORE-063 errors on a context call naming an undeclared place, and CORE-035 line 1 and CONC-026 line 2 forbid a firing to deposit outside its output places, so no relation of the joint model can witness the seam today); injection into a registered environment place that no arc touches needs RefExec's injection label (W5, ENV-002 AC2 and AC3). The quoted sentences restate AC3's first sentence only and leave the seams to the markdown. Its last sentence, that verification models such a place as one with no arcs whose tokens stay, is VER-001's subject; the Lean side is Novel.Seam.inertNet, which appends an arc-less place per inert place and adds no transition (inertNet_transitions).

AC4 (the SHOULD diagnostic: one WARN log-message event per distinct unknown place per executor, its logger, transition name and message) needs the event model (RefEvents, EVT-013, W7) and the events-wave rulings on payloads (D38) and wording (D20, clash evt-b#4 on the transition name); no quoted sentence states it and it is not encoded. Retention does not depend on it, as lines 3 and 4 show.

The test derivation is AC1 to AC3 on one net: CORE_072_nonvacuous starts from {1: 2 tokens, 2: 1 token, 9: 4 tokens} with 9 unknown, fires once, and keeps the unknown place's tokens unchanged, on counts and as the queue 90, 91, 92, 93; the WARN count is AC4's.

requirements.title: Marking Snapshot and Restore
requirements.statement:
fun {T} Snap Restore Seed ↦
  (∀ (F : FinQ String T), Restore (Snap F) = F.M) ∧
    (∀ (F : FinQ String T), QCanon (Snap F)) ∧
      (∀ (s : QSnap String T),
          QKeysNodup s → ∀ (k : String) (q : List T), (k, q) ∈ s → Restore s k = q) ∧
        (∀ (s : QSnap String T),
            QKeysNodup s → ∀ k ∉ List.map Prod.fst s, Restore s k = []) ∧
          (∀ (s E : QSnap String T),
              HoldsToken E → ∀ (M : QMarking String T), Seed (some s) E ≠ Except.ok M) ∧
            (∀ (s : QSnap String T), Seed (some s) [] = Except.ok (Restore s)) ∧
              ∀ (s E : QSnap String T) (M : QMarking String T),
                ¬HoldsToken E → Seed (some s) E = Except.ok M → M = Restore s
requirements.scope: all implementations; the seeding lines bind every executor that accepts a restored marking and an explicit initial marking together (Java, TypeScript)
reading: Let Snap be the snapshot (Snap F: the snapshot of the queue marking F.M, given with a finite list covering its marked places), Restore the restore (Restore s p: the queue the snapshot s restores on the place p) and Seed the seeding (Seed r E: the initial marking an executor is constructed with, from an optional restored snapshot r and an explicit initial marking E, or an error). Place names are strings.
For every F: Restore (Snap F) is F.M, on every place, token for token and in order.
For every F: Snap F is canonical (QCanon): its names are strictly ascending in String order, which is code-point order, and no entry has an empty queue.
For every snapshot s whose names are pairwise distinct and every entry (k, q) of s: Restore s k is q.
For every snapshot s whose names are pairwise distinct and every name k without an entry in s: Restore s k is empty.
For every snapshot s and every explicit initial marking E holding a token: Seed (some s) E is an error, for no marking M is it ok M.
For every snapshot s: Seed (some s) [] is ok (Restore s).
For every snapshot s, every explicit initial marking E holding no token and every marking M: if Seed (some s) E is ok M, then M is Restore s.
quotes: *When* a snapshot of a marking is restored, the restored marking *shall* hold on every place exactly the tokens the marking held there, in the same FIFO order, each token unchanged in its value and its `created_at`.
A snapshot an implementation returns to the host *shall* list its places in strictly ascending code-point order of the place name and *shall not* list a place that holds no token.

*When* a snapshot whose place names are pairwise distinct is restored, the restored marking *shall* hold on each place the snapshot names exactly the tokens of that place's entry, in their order, whatever the place name and whether or not the receiving net declares the place.
*When* a snapshot whose place names are pairwise distinct is restored, the restored marking *shall* hold no token on a place the snapshot does not name.

*If* an executor is constructed with a restored marking together with an explicit initial marking that holds a token, *then* the construction *shall* fail with an error to the caller, and the executor *shall not* merge the two markings or keep either one.
*When* an executor is constructed with a restored marking together with an explicit initial marking that names no place, the executor's initial marking *shall* be the restored marking.

*When* an executor is constructed with a restored marking together with an explicit initial marking that holds no token and the construction succeeds, the executor's initial marking *shall* be the restored marking.
*When* a restored marking seeds a new executor, each restored token *shall* keep its value and its `created_at`, whatever the executor's epoch clock ([TIME-015]).
assumes: The model is the triple (Snap, Restore, Seed) over the snapshot form QSnap String T (Reference/Snapshot.lean): a list of (place name, queue) entries, each queue the place's tokens in FIFO order, head oldest. T is the implementation's own token, its value and its created_at together, so 'the tokens are unchanged' covers both fields; the form imposes nothing on T, which is the fourth bullet of the form (an entry is the implementation's own token representation). A queue marking is a function, so a snapshot is taken of a FinQ: the marking with a finite list covering its marked places, which may repeat a name or name an unmarked place. The witness is refSnapshot (the marked places of the list, sorted by insertionSort, deduplicated, each with its whole queue), refRestore (the queue of the first entry for a name, else empty) and refSeed (ruling D84 (a)).

A snapshot is a mapping (the form's second paragraph), read as QKeysNodup: lines 3 and 4 range over snapshots whose names are pairwise distinct, which every runtime container (a Java Map, a TypeScript Map, a Rust BTreeMap, a Python dict) guarantees, and their quoted sentences say so ('a snapshot whose place names are pairwise distinct'). A list naming one place twice is not a snapshot, and no line constrains its restore.

Lines 1 and 2 with lines 3 and 4 pin both functions down: every triple meeting the block emits refSnapshot (core073_snapshot_eq) and restores every mapping as refRestore does (core073_restore_eq). The form's MUSTs on restore and emission follow as theorems for every such triple: a restore does not depend on the order the places appear in (core073_restore_perm), an entry with an empty queue restores like an absent one (core073_restore_dropEmpty), the snapshot depends only on the marking, not on the list it came with, so a drained place and a place that never held a token snapshot identically and snapshotting twice gives one artefact (core073_extensional), and it lists exactly the marked places (core073_keys).

Line 1 is the round trip (the body sentence, the first bullet of the form, the MUST NOT re-stamp sentence). Wrong models: a snapshot that reverses each queue violates it alone (CORE_073_mutant_roundTrip_killed); a restore that re-stamps every created_at (CORE_073_forbids_restampRestore, at T := value and created_at) and a snapshot written into a plain object that loses the name __proto__ (CORE_073_forbids_protoName, the reserved-name bullet) violate it too.

Line 2 is the emission half of the second bullet (omit a place with no token) and the canonical order paragraph (ascending code-point order of the place name), for the snapshot an implementation returns to the host: Snap is that operation. The same rule on a snapshot carried on an event (the paragraph 'The rule follows the form') is the event block's (EVT-014, W7), whose snapshot ruling D38 takes over the declared places; the rule does not reach a JSON session archive or the JSON debug protocol, which the quoted sentence therefore does not name. On String, Lean's order is lexicographic on characters, which is code-point order. A snapshot that keeps a drained place as an empty entry violates it alone (CORE_073_mutant_canonical_killed), and so does a snapshot sorted by UTF-16 code unit, on the names U+E000 and U+10000 (CORE_073_forbids_utf16).

Lines 3 and 4 are the restore half of the second bullet (accept a place omitted and a place present as an empty sequence, and restore them identically), the third bullet (a name the receiving net does not declare is retained: Restore knows no net, so every name is kept) and the fifth bullet (no name is reserved: line 3 holds at every string). A restore that accepts only the emitted form and restores nothing from a snapshot with an empty entry violates line 3 alone (CORE_073_mutant_restoreEntry_killed); a restore that keeps an earlier marking on the places a hand-authored snapshot omits violates line 4 alone (CORE_073_mutant_restoreAbsent_killed).

Lines 5, 6 and 7 are the paragraph 'A restore and an initial marking are two descriptions of one thing' and AC11, under ruling D84 (a): an explicit initial marking that holds a token is rejected together with a restore, an explicit initial marking that names no place is accepted and seeds the restored marking, and whenever a restore is accepted alongside an explicit marking that holds no token, the restored marking is what is seeded. A seed that silently prefers the restore violates line 5 alone (CORE_073_mutant_rejectBoth_killed), and so does a seed that merges the two (CORE_073_forbids_mergeSeed); a seed that refuses every restore, the shape the body's former 'supplying both' would force on a factory that always takes a map, violates line 6 alone (CORE_073_mutant_acceptEmpty_killed); a seed that accepts an explicit marking naming places with no token and then seeds that explicit marking, dropping every restored token (the selection written as 'initialTokens.isEmpty() ? restored : initialTokens'), violates line 7 alone (CORE_073_mutant_seedRestore_killed). Whether an explicit marking that names places but holds no token is rejected is left open (CORE_073_undecided_emptyEntries): refSeed accepts it, Java (initialTokens.isEmpty(), BitmapNetExecutor.java Builder.restore) and TypeScript (initialTokens.size > 0, bitmap-net-executor.ts) reject it, and both meet the block, line 7 included. Rust and Python take the restored marking as the initial marking itself and have no second input, so lines 5, 6 and 7 do not bind them (the scope). Seed is the seeding over nets without two places of one name: Java's build() rejects a restore into a net that declares two same-named places (Marking.resolveSnapshot, reached from Builder.seedTokens; MOD-024, AC10), which is the unmodelled N part below, so that rejection is not a counterexample to line 6.
The seeding lines say nothing of a seed without a restore: that the explicit initial marking is the initial marking is CORE-072's line 1.

Not modelled (N, Java only): the paragraph 'Restoring resolves names against the receiving net' (resolve each name against the net's declared places; retain an undeclared name under a placeholder place), the paragraph after it (reject, where the host asked, a snapshot or a restore over two places sharing one name; the marking-snapshot event never fails a run over it, EVT-014's) and AC10. Lean places are names, so a restore needs no net and is never ambiguous; Java's place equality over name and token type (MOD-024) forces it to take the net's places as a second input and to reject a snapshot or a restore over two same-named places, a divergence of Java's Place type, not of the form. Under ruling D21 the Kind line carries the primary kind only (F), so this N part is recorded here; a Java-scoped companion block is the integrator's call. The sixth bullet (no codec, the form is structural) and AC8 hold by type: every line is stated at every T, a function type included (core073_closure_roundTrip). The order rule's reach into events (EVT-014) and the reproducibility of JSON archives and the debug protocol (EVT-025) are the event blocks' (W7, W6), stated over the same refSnapshot. The non-normative note on the NU-022 tie-break and the SHOULD to reuse the canonical comparator are advice.

The VER paragraph ('A timed proof does not cross a restore') is a remark about proofs, cited by the VER blocks: the state-class graph of a resumed run starts from the initial state of CORE_073_T, every clock at zero; an untimed proof covers a restored marking taken from a real run at a moment with no work in flight (ENV-014, ruling R-CC6), not a hand-authored one.
AC1 (snapshot then restore round-trips each token's value and created_at) is line 1.

AC6 (FIFO order survives; the first firing takes A) is line 1 with the reference queue firing: CORE_073_nonvacuous restores A, B, C on a place and the reference delivery of a one-token input arc on it is A (EXEC-010).

AC7 (an empty place restores identically to an omitted one; an emitted snapshot omits empty places on every executor; an undeclared name is retained) is core073_restore_dropEmpty, line 2 with core073_extensional, and line 3. 'On every executor' is the scope: every snapshot an implementation emits is one Snap.
AC8 (no codec) is by type, as above. AC10 (resolution against the receiving net, rejection of two same-named places) is not modelled, as above.

AC9 (the engine does not re-stamp) is line 1 for the snapshot pair and CORE_073_forbids_restampRestore. The quoted sentence on seeding a new executor ('each restored token shall keep its value and its created_at, whatever the executor's epoch clock') is lines 6 and 7 for an executor that takes a restore and an explicit marking (Java, TypeScript): an accepted construction seeds Restore s itself, which by lines 1 and 3 is the snapshot's tokens unchanged, and Seed reads no clock, so no epoch clock can enter the seeded marking. For an executor whose initial marking is the restored marking itself (Rust, Python), the same sentence is the executor seeding its queues with the given tokens unchanged, which needs a timed state with tokens: the executor cycle relation's (RefExec, W5), which quotes the same sentence. AC2's 'exactly like any other initial marking' beyond counts is deferred there too.

AC11 (both is an error) is lines 5, 6 and 7, and AC12 (canonical place order: the same order twice, order-blind restore, ascending code-point order, also above U+FFFF) is line 2 with core073_extensional, core073_restore_perm and CORE_073_forbids_utf16.
AC2, AC3, AC4 and AC5 (the restored marking pre-populates places; the clocks start fresh at the resume) are the timed block CORE_073_T.

requirements.title: Marking Snapshot and Restore (resume timing)
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] Restore Rs ↦
  (∀ (X : TimedNet N) (s : QSnap N T) (now0 : ℕ), (Rs X s now0).m = qCount (Restore s)) ∧
    ∀ (X : TimedNet N) (s : QSnap N T) (now0 : ℕ) (u : Reference.Trans N),
      InNet X u →
        Enabled u (qCount (Restore s)) →
          (Rs X s now0).stamp u.core.name = some (ClockReading (Rs X s now0))
reading: Let Restore be the restore (Restore s: the queue marking the snapshot s restores) and Rs the resume (Rs X s now0: the timed state a new executor of the timed net X starts from when the snapshot s seeds it and its firing clock first reads now0).
For every timed net X, snapshot s and reading now0: the marking of Rs X s now0 is the token count of Restore s, on every place, declared or not.
For every timed net X, snapshot s, reading now0 and transition u of X that the counts of Restore s enable: u's stamp in Rs X s now0 is that state's own clock reading.
quotes: *When* a restored marking seeds a new executor, that executor's initial marking *shall* hold on every place the token count the restored marking holds there, whether or not the net declares the place ([CORE-072]).

*When* execution resumes from a restored marking, each transition of the net that the restored marking enables *shall* be armed with the firing clock's reading at that moment as its stamp, so that its elapsed time starts at 0 whatever the `created_at` of the restored tokens ([TIME-010]).
assumes: The model is the pair (Restore, Rs). Restore is CORE_073's restore, at any place type. Rs is the resume: like CORE-072's initialiser (glossary: Init), but from a snapshot, whose counts are all the timed state (TSt, Phase 1) carries. The witness is refRestore and refResume, the reference initialiser TSt.init on the counts of the restored marking at the resuming reading (Reference/Snapshot.lean). Armed, Elapsed time, Enabled and Unknown place are the glossary terms; transitions are identified by name (ruling D10, InNet).

Line 1 is the first quoted sentence and AC2 (a restored marking pre-populates places exactly like any other initial marking): on counts, on every place, the undeclared ones included (the third bullet of the form, CORE-072). A resume that keeps only the places the net lists violates it (CORE_073_T_mutant_marking_killed). That the restored tokens themselves, values and created_at, seed the executor's queues unchanged (AC9's executor side) needs a timed state with tokens, the executor cycle relation's (RefExec, W5).

Line 2 is the second quoted sentence, the paragraph 'The preserved created_at is token metadata' and the first sentence of the frequency paragraph ('Every restore restarts every clock', TIME-011): an enabled transition is stamped with the resumed state's own clock reading, so its elapsed time is 0 (core073T_elapsed) whatever the stamps of the restored tokens. With line 1 it is CORE-072's InitArms on the restored counts (core073T_initArms), and an initialiser that meets CORE-072 gives a resume that meets this block (core073T_of_core072). A resume that stamps from the tokens' created_at violates it (CORE_073_T_mutant_stamp_killed, at T := value and created_at), and so does a resume stamped when the executor was built, before the run starts (CORE_073_T_forbids_constructorStamp). As in CORE-072, the line fixes the stamp relative to the clock, not the clock reading itself: now0 is not constrained, so a resume that restarts its firing clock at 0 and stamps 0 meets the block, and is observationally equal under the reference timed step since elapsed time is a difference. How an injected epoch clock relates to the restored created_at (the NU-022 note) is TIME-015's. The line does not cover a terminal place marked by the restored marking (EXEC-042, RefExec).

AC3 (a Delayed or Window transition enabled by restored tokens waits its full interval from the resuming executor's enablement) is core073T_not_ready_after: after a delay shorter than the earliest bound from the resume, the transition is not ready under the reference timed step (TIME-010, TIME-004, TIME-005), and core073T_no_fire: it does not fire there. Both are shown for one delay step taken directly from the resumed state; several delay steps in a row, or firings of other transitions between the resume and the decision, are the reference timed step's own lines (TIME-010), which this block feeds with the resuming stamp.

AC4 (a Deadline(d) transition enabled by restored tokens is reaped once its elapsed time from the resuming stamp is strictly greater than d plus the deadline tolerance, ruling D4 and the AC4 rewording R-CC5) is core073T_expired_after: after one delay step from the resume, a reapable transition still enabled is expired exactly when the delay exceeds its latest bound plus the tolerance (TIME-003); that an expired transition is then reaped is TIME-013's step, not this block's. No TransitionTimedOut for the original budget is the event model's (EVT-009, W7); in this model no stamp survives the resume, so no original budget exists.

AC5 (restoring at an interval shorter than d never fires a Delayed(d) transition) is core073T_no_fire for one segment: each restore is a resume, and between two resumes less than d apart the clock advances by less than d, so the gate of TIME-010 is never passed. Restoring repeatedly is a sequence of such segments, each starting from a fresh resume; the block shows the segment, and the sequence is the host's loop, not a further line. The paragraph 'The fresh clock is safe for lower bounds and unsafe for upper bounds', its MUST NOT on the host, and the SHOULD to state the frequency bound are advice to hosts and implementations about the contract, not checkable lines.

requirements.title: Environment Place Registration
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T) (p : N) (x : T),
    (p ∉ C.envs →
        (∀ (r : Reply),
            on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.request p x r) s', shall fun x x_1 ↦
              r = Reply.error) ∧
          ∀ (r : Reply),
            on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.request p x r) s', shall fun s s' ↦ s' = s) ∧
      (p ∈ C.envs →
        ∀ (r : Reply),
          on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.request p x r) s', shall fun x x_1 ↦ r ≠ Reply.error)
requirements.scope: executors whose inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript)
reading: For every executor R, every configuration C, every place p and every token x:
if p is not one of C's environment places, a request step that asks to inject x into p answers with an error;
if p is not one of C's environment places, a request step that asks to inject x into p leaves the executor state as it was;
if p is one of C's environment places, a request step that asks to inject x into p does not answer with an error.
quotes: Environment places must be registered with the executor before execution begins.
The executor maintains a set of registered environment places.
Where inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), only registered environment places accept injections.
Where inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), attempting to inject into a non-environment place returns an error.
The set of registered environment places is fixed when the executor is built; no step of a run adds or removes one.

*Where* an executor's inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), *if* a caller injects into a place that is not a registered environment place, *then* the executor *shall* answer with an error, and *shall not* answer with a refusal even when it is draining, closed, stopped or finished.

*Where* an executor's inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), *if* a caller injects into a place that is not a registered environment place, *then* the executor *shall* leave its state unchanged: it *shall not* queue the token and *shall not* change the marking.

*Where* an executor's inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), the executor *shall* answer an injection into a place that is not a registered environment place with an error in every state of the run, before and after the run finishes.

*Where* an executor's inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), the executor *shall not* answer an injection into a registered environment place with an error, in any state of the run.

*Where* an executor's inject takes an environment-place handle (Java, TypeScript), *while* the run has not finished and the executor is not draining, closed or stopped, the executor *shall* accept an injection into a registered environment place.
assumes: The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. The label request p x r is the outside step of a caller asking to inject token x into place p, with the executor's answer r: accepted (queued), refused (the executor is draining, closed, stopped or finished, ENV-006) or error (not an environment place). The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean), whose request rule answers replyFor C s p and changes the state only on an accepted answer.

Scope (ruling D89 (a)): Java and TypeScript, whose inject takes an EnvironmentPlace handle and tests registration first (BitmapNetExecutor.inject and PrecompiledNetExecutor.inject return a failed future; the TypeScript inject rejects its promise and injectNoAwait throws). Rust and Python take a place name and deposit into the place it names whatever the registration (executor_handle.rs inject, executor_core/executor.rs handle_signal): the name-keyed executor env002_nameKeyed violates lines 1 and 2 (ENV_002_forbids_nameKeyed). For them the second block of this ID, ENV_002_host (kind A), states the host assumption instead.

The registered environment places are the configuration field C.envs (kind N): the quoted 'Environment places must be registered with the executor before execution begins.' and 'The executor maintains a set of registered environment places.' are that encoding. AC1 (the builder accepts registrations) is that field: every builder of the three languages fills it (Java Builder.environmentPlaces, TypeScript options.environmentPlaces, Rust ExecutorOptions.environment_places); it is configuration, not a step. That the reference's answer to an unregistered place depends on the configuration alone, in every state, is env002_registration_fixed (cited for ENV-001 AC3).

The quoted 'The set of registered environment places is fixed when the executor is built; no step of a run adds or removes one.' is lines 1 and 3 together: under ENV-002 a request step answers with an error exactly when its place is not in C.envs, in every state (env002_error_iff), so the registrations an executor honours are C.envs throughout the run. An executor that adds a place during a run breaks line 1. One that removes the registrations once a ticket has been drawn breaks line 3 (env002_shrinks, ENV_002_forbids_shrinks): the shape of a Java builder that keeps the caller's set instead of a copy, from which the host then removes a place. One that ignores the registrations and answers every injection with an error breaks line 3 (env002_neverMatches, ENV_002_forbids_neverMatches): the shape of a registration set built from the handles while inject tests the names.

Line 1 is the first EARS sentence. Its 'shall not answer with a refusal even when it is draining, closed, stopped or finished' is the order of the two tests: registration before the lifecycle, as Java (inject, then the closed and draining flags) and TypeScript (the throw, then the closed, draining and terminal flags) do. An executor that tests the lifecycle first answers a closed executor's unregistered injection with a refusal (ENV_002_forbids_lifecycleFirst). An executor that may answer a closed executor's unregistered injection with a refusal besides the error breaks line 1 only (ENV_002_mutant_mayRefuse). 'Answer with an error' also excludes an acceptance, which is the 'only' of AC2: an accepted request names a registered place (env002_only_registered_accept, cited for AC2).

Line 2 is the second EARS sentence: the request changes nothing, so no token is queued (the event queue XSt.eq is unchanged), the marking is unchanged and the loop is not woken (XSt.parked is unchanged). An executor that answers with an error and still queues the token breaks line 2 only (ENV_002_mutant_errorButQueue).

Its offers are in ExecCoversW5.Env002Covers (ConsistencyExec.lean; the convention of GlossaryExec.lean: offers are coverage clauses, never block lines). The third and the fifth EARS sentences demand an answer and are quoted whole; their safety halves are lines 1 and 3, and their existence halves are that clause. The third EARS sentence and the 'returns' of AC3 say the error is an answer the executor gives in every state, open, draining, closed, stopped or after the run finished, not a call that blocks: Env002Covers offers it in every executor state, reachable or not, which is more than 'every state of the run' and which the reference meets (env002_ref_covers). An executor without a request step for an unregistered place satisfies every line and fails that clause (env002_covers_noAnswer); it is also the reference restricted to a host that meets ENV_002_host, which is why a name-keyed executor under that assumption is indistinguishable from the reference on the host's runs.

Line 3 is the fourth EARS sentence: a registered place is never answered with an error, in any state; once the executor is draining, closed, stopped or finished the answer is a refusal (ENV-006), a false future in Java and false in TypeScript. An executor that may answer a registered place with an error besides the reference's answer breaks line 3 only (env002_mayErrorRegistered, ENV_002_mutant_mayErrorRegistered): the shape of a registration test by object identity that misses an equal handle the caller built anew.

The fifth EARS sentence, the 'accept' of AC2 and the 'success' of the test derivation, is the second half of Env002Covers: while the executor is open (not draining, closed or stopped) and in a phase of the run (isExecPhase, not finished), R offers to accept an injection into a registered place. That clause requires the accepting step to exist; that an open running executor never refuses a registered place instead is ENV-010's line 2, and what the accepted request does (queue the token with a ticket, FIFO) is ENV-003's. An executor that refuses every registered place meets every line and fails the clause (env002_refuseRegistered, env002_covers_refuseRegistered): the shape of a lifecycle flag that starts set. Injections before the run starts are outside the model, whose runs start at xinit in mode open.

AC1 is the configuration field C.envs, and line 3 and Env002Covers say the executor honours it. AC2 is line 1 for 'only' and Env002Covers for 'accept'. AC3 is line 1 and Env002Covers. AC4 is the second block, ENV_002_host. A refusal is ENV-006's subject, on the same request label. The Java error is a failed future and the TypeScript error a rejected promise (inject) or a thrown exception (injectNoAwait); the model does not tell them apart, all are the answer error.

The test derivation's Java and TypeScript clause (register 3 environment places; inject into a registered one, success; inject into an unregistered one, error) is ENV_002_nonvacuous: with places 0, 1 and 2 registered, a request into 0 is accepted and its token lands in place 0 at the next injection step, a request into 0 by the closed executor is refused, not answered with an error, and a request into place 3 is answered with an error, by an open and by a closed executor, with the state unchanged. Its Rust and Python clause (AC4 is an assumption on the host, which no executor test checks) is the kind A of the second block.

requirements.title: Environment Place Registration (host of a name-keyed inject)
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} C tr ↦
  ∀ st ∈ tr, ∀ (p : N) (x : T) (r : Reply), st.2.1 = XLbl.request p x r → p ∈ C.envs
requirements.scope: executors whose inject takes a place name (Rust, Python), and their hosts
reading: For a configuration C and a run tr (a list of steps, each a source state, a label and a target state):
every request step of tr asks to inject into one of C's environment places.
quotes: Where inject takes a place name (Rust, Python), the host injects only into registered environment places.

An executor whose inject takes a place name (Rust, Python) deposits an injected token into the place the name resolves to, whether or not that place is registered; for it, registration decides only whether the run waits at quiescence ([ENV-010]) and which arcs the dead-arc report lists ([CORE-037]).
*Where* an executor's inject takes a place name (Rust, Python), the host *shall* inject only into registered environment places.
assumes: Ruling D89 (a). The block is an assumption on the host (kind A), not a behaviour of the executor: a Rust or Python executor answers a request into any place, deposits into the place the name resolves to (an unknown one is retained, CORE-072), and registration feeds only the long-running decision (ENV-010) and the dead-arc report (CORE-037, rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor.rs). The statement reads only the labels of a run, so it is a predicate on what the host asks, whatever executor answers.

What the assumption buys is env002_host_transfer: every run of the name-keyed executor env002_nameKeyed (the reference with the registration test removed from its answer, the Rust and Python shape) that meets ENV_002_host is a run of the reference executor RefExec, so every property proved of RefExec runs (the first block of this ID included) holds of the name-keyed executor on the runs of a host that meets it. The assumption is load-bearing: a name-keyed run with one request into an unregistered place is not a run of the reference (env002_host_needed). The verifier's open-system model makes the same assumption (Novel.EnvSemantics.StepCE injects only into a registered environment place), and CORE-037 states it for the dead-arc report ('a host injects tokens only into environment places').

The second quoted sentence describes the name-keyed executor; it is the model env002_nameKeyed, not a line. AC4 is the one line, and the test derivation's Rust and Python clause says no executor test checks it. AC1 to AC3 and the test derivation's Java and TypeScript clause are the first block's.

requirements.title: inject() Thread Safety
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (∀ (p : N) (x : T),
        on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.request p x Reply.accepted) s', shall fun s s' ↦
          s' =
            { M := s.M, now := s.now, cyc := s.cyc, st := s.st, fl := s.fl,
              nextId := s.nextId + 1, cq := s.cq, pq := s.pq,
              eq := s.eq ++ [(s.nextId, p, x)], mode := s.mode, phase := s.phase,
              order := s.order, delta := s.delta, started := s.started,
              parked := false }) ∧
      (∀ (k : ℕ),
          on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.inject k) s', shall fun s s' ↦
            ∃ p x rest,
              s.eq = (k, p, x) :: rest ∧ s'.eq = rest ∧ s'.M = qAppendOne s.M p x) ∧
        (∀ (l : XLbl N T),
            Env003.keepsQueue l = true →
              on fun s s' ↦ R C s l s', shall fun s s' ↦ s'.eq = s.eq) ∧
          (∀ (l : XLbl N T),
              Env003.dropsQueue l = true →
                on fun s s' ↦ R C s l s', shall fun s s' ↦ s'.eq.Sublist s.eq) ∧
            (∀ (l : XLbl N T),
                on fun s s' ↦ R C s l s', shall fun s s' ↦ s.nextId ≤ s'.nextId) ∧
              ∀ (s0 : XSt N T) (k : ℕ),
                on-ideal-runs IdealRun R C s0, shall
                  when Env003.accepts k, shall Env003.serves C k
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C:

an accepted request of token x into place p leaves the state as it was except that the event queue gains (n, p, x) at its tail, n the ticket supply's value before the step, the supply moves on to n + 1, and the parked flag is cleared;
an injection with ticket k happens only when the event queue starts with an entry (k, p, x): it leaves the rest of the queue and adds x at the tail of place p, every other place unchanged;
every step that is not an accepted request, an injection, a discard, an immediate termination or a finish leaves the event queue as it was;
a discard, an immediate termination and a finish leave an event queue that is a sublist of the one before (entries removed, the others kept in order);
no step lowers the ticket supply;

for every start state and every ticket k, on every run that reaches its finish, a step that accepts a request under ticket k is followed, at it or later, by the injection of k, a close, an immediate termination or a finish on a terminal place from a state where a terminal place is marked.
quotes: The inject operation is safe to call from any thread, task, or coroutine — not just the orchestrator thread.
It enqueues the token for processing on the next orchestrator cycle.

*When* the executor accepts an `inject()` call, it *shall* append the event to the tail of its queue of accepted events, as a new entry under a fresh ticket that identifies the call, and *shall not* change the marking or any other part of its state, except that it moves its ticket supply on and wakes the orchestrator if it is waiting ([ENV-005]).

*When* the orchestrator injects an accepted event, it *shall* take the oldest entry of the queue, *shall* remove that entry from the queue, *shall* add its token at the tail of its place (glossary: Queue order) and *shall not* change any other place.

The executor *shall not* change its queue of accepted events in any other way than appending a newly accepted event, injecting the oldest entry, discarding entries once it is closed ([ENV-013]) or terminated immediately ([ENV-015]), and emptying the queue when the run ends ([EXEC-041]), so that it injects accepted events in the order it accepted them.

*When* the executor discards queued events or the run ends, the executor *shall* only remove entries from its queue of accepted events and *shall* keep the remaining entries in the order it accepted them.
The executor *shall not* move its ticket supply back, so that no two accepted calls share a ticket.

*When* the executor accepts an `inject()` call, the orchestrator *shall* inject its token before the run finishes, unless after accepting it the executor is closed ([ENV-013]), is terminated immediately ([ENV-015]) or stops because a terminal place is marked ([EXEC-042]).

*While* the orchestrator is in the external-events step of a cycle ([EXEC-001] step 2), no terminal place is marked, the executor is neither closed ([ENV-013]) nor terminated immediately ([ENV-015]) and its queue of accepted events is not empty, the orchestrator *shall* inject the oldest entry.
assumes: The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. A caller's inject() is the outside step request p x r with the reply r; the event queue eq holds the accepted events with their tickets, drawn from the supply nextId that firing identities share. The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean), the graph of a step function checked rule by rule against the Rust executor.

AC1 and AC2 (inject() callable from a thread other than the orchestrator's, concurrent calls without data races) are kind Q: threads, locks and memory visibility are not in the model. The model reads them at the grain of interleaving: request is an outside step (CONC-001), offered by the reference in every phase of a running loop, so an injection can arrive between any two executor steps; that it is offered at all is coverage of the consistency theorem, not a line here. The Java ConcurrentLinkedQueue, the TypeScript single thread and the Rust FIFO channel are what make the step atomic, and the tests are the evidence (coverage matrix: Rust only).

The first quoted sentence ('safe to call from any thread') is AC1 and AC2, kind Q as above. The second ('It enqueues the token for processing on the next orchestrator cycle') is lines 1 and 6 and the coverage clause Env003Covers. Line 1 is the enqueue: the token does not land in the marking at the call (ENV_003_forbids_atCall: the Novel spike ApplyInPlace). Env003Covers is the processing: in step 2, with no terminal place marked and the executor neither closed nor stopped, the orchestrator can inject the oldest queued event (env003_covers_noInject: a step 2 that never injects is stuck with the event queued, a run that never finishes, which line 6 alone does not see; it meets every line and fails the clause). The cycle position is EXEC-001's and CONC-010's: an event queued when step 2 begins is injected before that cycle's enablement update (EXEC-001 line 5, step 2 ends only with an empty queue), and the wait never parks with an event queued (CONC-010 line 1, ENV-005). Ruling D70 (a) and clash env-a#8: Rust injects in the wait as well as in step 2 (the wait's signal arm), so lines 2 and 6 say 'the orchestrator injects it', never which phase; the reference offers inject in step 2 and in the wait, and Env003Covers asks only for step 2.

The first EARS sentence is line 1: an accepted request changes only the event queue, by appending its entry at the tail (ENV_003_forbids_headQueue: a stack), the ticket supply, by moving on so that the entry has a ticket of its own (ENV_003_forbids_reusesTicket: two queued entries share a ticket, so ENV-004 cannot tell their answers apart), and the parked flag, which it clears: 'wakes the orchestrator if it is waiting' reads as the flag false after the step, a loop that was blocked is woken and one that was not stays unblocked (ENV_003_forbids_noWake: an accepted request that leaves a blocked loop blocked). ENV-005 line 3 says the same of the flag; ENV-005 builds on this block (its Depends on line names ENV-003), so the [ENV-005] of the sentence is a cross-reference, and ENV-005 is not in this block's Depends on line. Whether a request is accepted, refused or answered with an error is ENV-002's and ENV-006's subject; this block constrains the accepted ones.

The second EARS sentence is line 2, the new sentence of ruling D48 (a) (events FIFO by acceptance, appended at the tail): an injection takes the head of the queue (ENV_003_forbids_newestFirst), removes it (ENV_003_forbids_keepsQueued: the same event would be injected again) and appends its token at the tail of its place, the glossary's queue order for a deposit (ENV_003_forbids_headOfPlace). The line fixes the marking exactly (qAppendOne), which is the sentence's 'shall not change any other place'. That an injected token writes its place, so a reaped transition with an arc on it is no longer reaped (ruling D6), is the glossary Write entry and TIME-013's companion line; where the loop goes after an injection from the wait is EXEC-001's.

The third EARS sentence is line 3 and the fourth is line 4. Line 3: no step other than an accepted request, an injection, a discard, an immediate termination or a finish changes the queue (ENV_003_forbids_perPlaceQueues: one queue per place drains place by place and loses the order across places; ENV_003_forbids_clearsAtEnd: an end of step 2 that empties the queue, the TypeScript walk of a fixed prefix followed by clearing the whole queue, drops an event accepted during the walk). Line 4: a discard, an immediate termination and a finish only remove entries and keep the rest in order (ENV_003_forbids_rotates: a discard that moves the head to the tail keeps every event and passes lines 3 and 6). With lines 1 and 2 they give FIFO by acceptance. When a discard may come (only once the executor is closed or stopped) is ENV-004 line 2 and ENV-013; the immediate termination that drops the whole queue is ENV-015; the finish empties the queue (EXEC-041; ENV-004 for the answer each dropped call gets). The reference meets line 4: discard removes the head, and terminateNow and every finish set the queue to empty. A refused request is a step that keeps the queue, as ENV-006 also says. A close keeps the queue and later discard steps drop it, as the Java and TypeScript loops do; Java's close() on an executor whose loop is not running completes the queued calls with false at once (BitmapNetExecutor.close), which the model does not reach: it has no state before the loop starts, and after the finish the queue is already empty.

The fifth EARS sentence is line 5, the 'fresh ticket' of the first: the supply never goes back, so with line 1 every accepted call gets a ticket no earlier call of the run had. Firing identities draw from the same supply (a start moves it on), so the line also reads EXEC-031's identity supply; the reference never lowers it. The line is load-bearing for line 6, whose watch keeps one flag per ticket: an executor that resets the supply at the enablement update and whose termination test forgets the event queue accepts 7 and 8 under the same ticket 0, injects the 7, and finishes with the 8 never injected and no close, while one injection of ticket 0 pays both acceptances (ENV_003_forbids_resetsSupply). Line 6 reads every start state, including ones whose queue already holds a ticket at or above the supply; from a start state whose queued tickets are distinct and below the supply (every initial state; ENV-004's env004_Fresh), lines 1 to 5 keep them so.

The sixth EARS sentence is line 6 and the reading of AC3. The markdown's AC3 carries the exception (clash env-a#7, ruling D20): ENV-013 and EXEC-042 drop queued events, so a close (ENV-013), an immediate termination (ENV-015, Java) or a stop because a terminal place is marked (EXEC-042) after the acceptance releases the executor. The reference shows the exception is needed: ENV_003_allows_closeDiscards decides a reference run that finishes with an accepted event discarded after a close. A terminal stop releases only when a terminal place is marked in the state it starts from (Env003.serves): ENV_003_forbids_latchTerminal is the TypeScript terminal latch moved from processExternalEvents into inject() (or Java's isTerminal test next to externalEventQueue.offer), which stops the loop when an event for a terminal place is accepted, before its token is in the marking, and drops an event accepted earlier for another place; EXEC-042's last line catches it too. Rust injects every event sent before its close (one FIFO channel for events and the close signal); that is a run whose close step comes after those injections, and line 6 holds of it either way.

Line 6 is liveness read on runs that reach their finish (IdealRun, an assumption of kind A of glossary GlossaryExec.lean): on a finite run 'eventually' reads 'before the finish'. A run of an open executor with environment places that is never drained or closed does not finish, and line 6 says nothing about it; there, Env003Covers says the injection is always on offer in step 2, and that the loop takes it rather than stalling is the loop's own fairness, outside the model. Line 6 is load-bearing beyond lines 1 to 5: an executor whose termination test forgets the event queue finishes quiescent with an accepted event never injected (ENV_003_forbids_forgets), the Java or TypeScript loop exit reading only the transitions and the actions in flight. ENV_003_nonvacuous decides reference runs that finish after an injection, so the assumption holds of some runs and the line is not vacuous (onIdealRuns_of_none).

Its offers are in ExecCoversW5.Env003Covers (ConsistencyExec.lean; the convention of GlossaryExec.lean: offers are coverage clauses, never block lines). The seventh EARS sentence demands an answer and is quoted whole; it has no safety half, and its existence half is that clause: the inject step of the oldest entry exists in every such state, which the reference meets by its inject rule (env003_ref_covers); other steps (a request, a snapshot) may come first, and nothing ends step 2 while an event is queued (EXEC-001 line 5). Depends on: ENV-002 (which places accept), ENV-013, ENV-015, EXEC-041 and EXEC-042 (the releases and drops of lines 3, 4 and 6), EXEC-001 (step 2) and CONC-010 (the wait).

Scope: Rust run_sync has no signal channel and no inject() (spec/06-environment-places.md, ENV-014's implementation status), so the requirement reads the executors that accept injections. Python rides on the Rust runtime.

The test derivation (ten threads each inject a token, all ten are processed) is ENV_003_nonvacuous, part 5: ten requests are accepted, the executor drains, the ten tokens are injected in the order they were accepted and land at the tail of place 0 behind its initial token, and the run finishes quiescent; the threads are AC1 and AC2.

requirements.title: inject() Completion Semantics
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (∀ (k : ℕ),
        (on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.inject k) s', shall fun s s' ↦
            ∃ p x, (k, p, x) ∈ s.eq ∧ s'.M = qAppendOne s.M p x) ∧
          (∀ (s : XSt N T) (l : XLbl N T) (s' : XSt N T),
              R C s l s' →
                env004_isDrop k (s, l, s') = true →
                  s'.M = s.M ∧ (s'.mode.closing = true ∨ isExecPhase s'.phase = false)) ∧
            ∀ (s0 : XSt N T) (tr : List (XStep N T)),
              env004_Fresh s0 → XRun R C s0 tr → (at-most-once env004_answers k) tr) ∧
      on fun s s' ↦ env004_Fresh s ∧ ∃ p x, R C s (XLbl.request p x Reply.accepted) s',
        shall fun s s' ↦ ∃ j ∉ env004_tickets s, j ∈ env004_tickets s'
requirements.scope: executors with an admission signal (Java, TypeScript); Rust and Python report acceptance only (ruling D44 (a))
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C, and in the first three lines for every ticket k:

an inject step of k (the admission signal of k completes with true) starts in a state whose event queue holds an event with ticket k for some place p and token x, and its marking is the source marking with x appended at the tail of p and no other change;

a step that removes the ticket k from the event queue and is not the inject step of k (the signal completes with false) leaves the marking unchanged, and after it the executor is closed or stopped, or the run has finished;

on every run of R that starts in a state whose queued events carry pairwise distinct tickets, each below the ticket supply, at most one step answers k (injects it, or removes it from the queue otherwise);
an accepted injection request made in a state whose queued events carry pairwise distinct tickets, each below the ticket supply, leaves some ticket queued that was not queued before it.
quotes: In Java and TypeScript the inject operation returns a future/promise that completes with true when the token has been added to the marking.
In Rust and Python the return value indicates whether the injection was accepted; in Java and TypeScript the future's value indicates whether the token was injected.
In Java and TypeScript the future is the admission signal of the accepted event.
The orchestrator completes it with true in the external-events step ([EXEC-001] step 2), when it adds the token to the marking.
It completes it with false when it discards the event because the executor is closed or stopped ([ENV-013], [ENV-015]), or when the run ends with the event still queued ([EXEC-041], [EXEC-042]).
A drain does not discard the events accepted before it: the orchestrator still injects them ([ENV-011]), unless close() is called or the run ends first.
Each accepted event has an admission signal of its own: an injection into a place whose earlier event is still queued neither replaces that event nor merges with it ([ENV-003]).
*When* the executor accepts an injection request, it *shall* queue the event as a new event, apart from every event already queued.

*When* the executor completes the admission signal of an accepted event with true, it *shall*, in the same step, add the event's token at the tail of its place's queue and change no other part of the marking.
*If* the executor completes the admission signal of an accepted event with false, *then* it *shall* leave the marking unchanged in that step.
*If* a step leaves the executor open or draining and does not end the run, *then* the executor *shall not* complete the admission signal of an accepted event with false in that step.
The executor *shall* complete the admission signal of an accepted event at most once.
assumes: The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. An accepted request (request p x accepted, ENV-003, ENV-006) queues the event (k, p, x) in s.eq with the ticket k = s.nextId and advances the supply. The admission signal is not part of the state: the block reads it off the steps. The true answer of ticket k is the label inject k; the false answer is every other step after which k is no longer queued. In the reference those are discard k (once the executor is closed or stopped), terminateNow (ENV-015, ruling D47 (c): Java completes the queued events with false inside terminateNow) and the finish steps that clear the queue (finish closed, stopped or terminal; design R17). The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean).

One signal for ENV-004 and ENV-006. ENV-006's line 4 and this block both name the answering steps by what they do to the queue (the injection of k, or a step that takes the event with ticket k out of the event queue): ENV-006's answersTicket and this block's env004_answers are equal on every step (env004_answers_eq_answersTicket, ConsistencyExec.lean), which is what lets lines 1 and 2 constrain the value and the marking effect of every answer ENV-006 asks for. On every reference step from a state with distinct queued tickets both also agree with a label-based restatement, env004_labelAnswers (the injection or the discard of k, or an immediate termination or a finish while k is queued; ENV_004_answers_agree_reference), so the reference answers one ticket at one step in both blocks.

Scope, ruling D44 (a). Only Java and TypeScript have an admission signal, as the first two quoted sentences now say. Rust and Python return, at the call, whether the event was accepted; that reply is the request step's, stated by ENV-006 (and ENV-002 for a place that is not an environment place). The quoted second sentence keeps the two meanings apart: the call's reply says whether the request was accepted (ENV-006's lines 1 and 2), the future's value says whether the token was injected (lines 1 and 2 here), so an accepted event can still be answered false. A run of RefExec in which the close comes after the injections of the events sent before it is Rust's behaviour at a close (ruling D44 (a)), so the shared model holds both. Result-less forms (Java injectAsync, TypeScript injectNoAwait) have no signal to complete and are outside the block.

Ruling D44 (a), from env-a ENV-R3: the old clause that the signal completes after enablement has been recalculated is dropped. Java and TypeScript complete the signal inside the external-events step, before the enablement update of step 3, and line 1 reads exactly that step: the inject step is the one that deposits. The quoted first, third and fourth sentences are line 1 for what the answering step changes. Which loop phase the inject step runs in is EXEC-001's subject, not this block's: EXEC-001's line 5 orders the injections of step 2 before the next update, and ruling D70 (a) lets the wait itself inject (Rust, which has no signal; the reference offers inject in the phases events and await). Line 1 therefore has no phase condition, and the step-2 placement in the fourth quoted sentence is checked there.

AC1 (true when the token is in the marking) is line 1: the inject step of k appends the event's token at the tail of its place and changes the marking in no other way. An executor that answers true and lands the token later, through another queue, breaks it (ENV_004_forbids_earlyTrue). The first part of ENV_004_nonvacuous is the test derivation: a request is accepted, the event is injected, and after the answer the token is in its place.

AC2 has two halves. The call-time half, an inject() call made while the executor is draining, closed or finished is refused and changes nothing, is ENV-006's lines 1 and 2 (ENV_006.lean: Refusing is a mode that is not open, or a finished run, which is where the 'or finished' of AC2 comes from); this block does not restate it. The queued half is line 2 and the quoted fifth sentence: an accepted event is answered false only once the executor is closed or stopped, or when the run ends with the event still queued (ENV_004_nonvacuous parts three and four), and the false answer leaves the marking unchanged (ENV_004_forbids_discardDeposits). AC2's drain clause and the quoted drain sentence are line 2's mode half: while the executor drains and the run goes on, no queued event is answered false. An executor that discards a queued event because the executor is draining when step 2 reaches it breaks that half (ENV_004_forbids_falseWhileDraining), while the reference injects an event accepted before a drain and answers it true (ENV_004_nonvacuous part two). The clause allows a false answer during a drain when the run ends (a terminal place marked, EXEC-042) or close() escalates the drain (ENV-013), which is why AC2 does not promise true for every event queued before a drain. That such an event is in the end injected is ENV-011's and ENV-006's line 4, not this block's.

AC3 (at most once) is line 3 and the last quoted sentence. An executor that injects the event but leaves it queued, then discards it at a close, answers it twice (true, then false) and breaks only line 3 (ENV_004_forbids_trueThenDiscard, env004_trueThenDiscard_onlyLine3). The line identifies the event by its ticket. Tickets are drawn once from one supply (the naming convention of the glossary, shared with firing identities), and the premise says that at the start of the run the queued tickets are distinct and below the supply: true at every initial state (the queue is empty) and kept by every reference step (env004_fresh_shape). Without it the reference itself answers a duplicated ticket twice (env004_needs_fresh). An executor that hands out a ticket already queued answers it twice along the run and breaks line 3 as well.

Line 4 is the quoted sentence on an admission signal of its own and the EARS sentence on queueing the event as a new event. Without it an executor that keeps the pending injections per place, so that a second accepted request into the same place overwrites the first event's token under the first event's ticket, keeps lines 1 to 3 (env004_coalesce_onlyLine4: no ticket ever leaves the queue without its inject step), yet one of the two callers told accepted never sees its token reach the marking. Line 4 rejects it (ENV_004_forbids_coalesce). ENV-003's line 1 pins the exact ticket (the supply's next one), the place, the token and the FIFO position of the new event (ruling D48 (a)); line 4 keeps only what the signal needs, a ticket of its own.

Lines 2 and 3 together say that a token answered false never reaches the marking through its own event: the drop leaves the marking unchanged, and no later inject step answers the same ticket. The quoted sentences on which events a close discards are ENV-013's subject, the FIFO order of injection is ENV-003's (ruling D48 (a)), and that every accepted event is eventually answered is ENV-006's line 4; this block reads only the answering step and what it changes.

Out of the model: a deposit that throws, which Java and TypeScript report by completing the signal exceptionally (the model's deposit cannot fail, so line 3 says at most one answer, not exactly one); the TokenAdded event of the injection (the event tier, W7). Java and TypeScript leave the events queued at a close and complete them with false when the loop ends, after the firings in flight; the reference discards them in step 2 of the cycles after the close. Both are after the close and before the end of the run, and line 2 constrains only which step answers false and what it changes, not how long after the close it comes.

requirements.title: inject() Wake-Up
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (while fun s ↦ s.eq ≠ [], never fun s s' ↦ ∃ tmr, R C s (XLbl.park tmr) s') ∧
      (while fun s ↦ s.eq ≠ [], never fun s s' ↦
          s.parked = false ∧ s'.parked = true ∧ ∃ l, R C s l s') ∧
        (∀ (p : N) (x : T),
            on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.request p x Reply.accepted) s', shall fun x s' ↦
              s'.parked = false) ∧
          (while fun s ↦ s.eq ≠ [], never fun s s' ↦ R C s XLbl.endEvents s') ∧
            while fun s ↦ s.eq ≠ [], never fun s s' ↦
              s.phase ≠ Phase.update ∧ s'.phase = Phase.update ∧ ∃ l, R C s l s'
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C:
