The deferred arm is an answer step taken after that firing settled and its published tokens were deposited (Rust and Python serve the request of an inline synchronous action at the next cycle), which may be some false when nothing else is in flight; the block allows it. That the orchestrator does not park against itself, that the deferred reply is not blocked on from the orchestrator's own thread of control, and the body's 'An implementation with that shape MUST detect the case and capture directly on the calling thread, after whatever synchronisation of internal token storage any other marking read performs' (the inline-action form of the same duty) are thread properties (kind Q): the model has no threads, and a step relation cannot wait for itself.

AC9: a parked executor answers without waking: line 1 keeps the parked flag and the phase of an answer in the wait (ENV_014_nonvacuous part 3 answers from a parked state and stays parked, and ENV_014_forbids_wakingSnapshot breaks it), and that the answer carries the current marking is the modelling assumption of the second paragraph. 'Without the orchestrator's participation' (Java's park epoch, Rust's race of the clock's wait against its signal channel) is a thread property (kind Q). AC9's marking() half is not a step of the model: a foreign marking() read is a read of s.M, current by construction, and its thread half is kind Q under ruling D43 (a), which CONC-001's block records for foreign reads. The last published marking of Java's unserved request after its 2 s best-effort cap (ruling D43 (a), ENVB-R4 (a)) is an answer whose marking is earlier than the state's, outside the model by the second paragraph; its flag is forced true, which is the duty the second paragraph accounts for.

Kind Q, outside the lines: AC2's 'within one orchestrator cycle' is a latency, which rests on coverage (the reference offers an answer at entry to every enablement update, env014_snapshot_offered, so a request is answered in the cycle it arrives in or in the wait); AC2's 'keeps running afterwards' is line 1 (the answer changes neither the mode nor the phase). AC3 (an owned copy, independent of subsequent executor state) is a property of the returned value: in the model the marking of an answer is a value, so later steps cannot change it; aliasing is tested, not proven. Java's 2 s cap and 50 ms recheck are implementation choices (kind N).

CORE-073: a restore-point answer restores, through the snapshot form, to the marking of the state it was taken from, with nothing in flight and nothing queued (env014_restorePoint_restores). The test derivation's second half (snapshot again at quiescence and restore to an equivalent marking) is that theorem together with ENV_014_nonvacuous part 2. The guarantee 'restore and resume' needs CORE-073's own block for the seeding (refSeed).

requirements.title: Immediate Termination
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (∀ (l : XLbl N T),
        on fun s s' ↦ s.mode ≠ Mode.stopped ∧ s'.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ R C s l s', shall
          fun x x_1 ↦ l = XLbl.terminateNow) ∧
      (∀ (l : XLbl N T),
          on fun s s' ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ R C s l s', shall fun x s' ↦
            s'.mode = Mode.stopped) ∧
        (on fun s s' ↦ R C s XLbl.terminateNow s', shall fun s s' ↦
            s'.mode = Mode.stopped ∧
              s'.M = s.M ∧ s'.phase = s.phase ∧ s'.eq = [] ∧ s'.parked = false) ∧
          (∀ (p : N) (x : T) (r : Reply),
              on fun s s' ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ R C s (XLbl.request p x r) s', shall
                fun x x_1 ↦ r ≠ Reply.accepted) ∧
            (while fun s ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped, never fun s s' ↦
                ∃ k, R C s (XLbl.inject k) s') ∧
              (while fun s ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped, never fun s s' ↦
                  ∃ i,
                    ¬(s.phase = Phase.pass ∧ ∃ f ∈ s.fl, f.id = i ∧ f.sync = true) ∧
                      (R C s (XLbl.commit i) s' ∨
                        R C s (XLbl.fail i) s' ∨ R C s (XLbl.tdeposit i) s')) ∧
                (while fun s ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ s.phase = Phase.completions, never
                    fun s s' ↦
                    ∃ l,
                      l.outside = false ∧
                        (∀ (a : Option Bool), l ≠ XLbl.snapshot a) ∧
                          (∀ (c : Cause), l ≠ XLbl.finish c) ∧ R C s l s') ∧
                  (on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.finish Cause.stopped) s', shall fun s s' ↦
                      s.phase = Phase.completions ∧ s'.M = s.M ∧ s'.eq = []) ∧
                    (while fun s ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ s.phase ≠ Phase.publications,
                        never fun s s' ↦ ∃ i, R C s (XLbl.publish i) s') ∧
                      on fun s s' ↦ s.mode = Mode.stopped ∧ R C s XLbl.endPass s', shall
                        fun s x ↦ s.order = []
requirements.scope: all executors; the operation itself is optional (MAY) and only Java provides it
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C, where an executor state is stopped when its lifecycle mode is stopped:
a step that leads from a state that is not stopped to a stopped state is a terminateNow step;
every step from a stopped state leads to a stopped state;
a terminateNow step leads to a stopped state, leaves the marking and the phase unchanged, empties the queue of external events and clears the parked flag;
a request step from a stopped state is not answered accepted;
while the state is stopped, R takes no inject step;
while the state is stopped, R takes no commit, fail or tdeposit step of a firing i, unless the phase is the firing pass and a synchronous firing with identity i is in flight;
while the state is stopped and its phase is completions (the start of a cycle), R takes no executor step other than a finish, except an answer to a snapshot request;
a finish stopped step starts in phase completions, leaves the marking unchanged and empties the queue of external events;
while the state is stopped and its phase is not publications (step 1b), R takes no publish step;
an endPass step from a stopped state starts with an empty ready order.
quotes: An implementation MAY provide an immediate-termination operation (`terminateNow()`) that stops the orchestrator loop **without** waiting for in-flight actions, unlike `close()` ([ENV-013]) which lets them complete.
New `inject()` calls are rejected (return error / false), as after [ENV-013].
Queued external events are discarded (completed with false).
The loop stops at the end of its current cycle; it does NOT wait for in-flight actions, and their results are discarded rather than admitted to the marking.
In-flight actions keep running where the runtime cannot cancel them ([IO-013]); their consumed tokens are lost ([EXEC-031]).
It is an explicit escape hatch and MUST NOT be invoked implicitly by `close()`.
The executor is **stopped** from the moment `terminateNow()` takes effect.
The call takes effect between two steps of the loop ([EXEC-001]): a call that lands while a step is under way takes effect when that step ends.
The current cycle is the one under way when the call takes effect; it ends where the next cycle would start, before its step 1.
A request that lands before the call takes effect may still be accepted; its event is then discarded, and its admission completes with `false` ([ENV-004]).
*When* `terminateNow()` takes effect, the executor *shall* become stopped, *shall* discard every external event still queued ([ENV-004]) and *shall* end a wait under way in step 6 ([CONC-010]).

*When* `terminateNow()` takes effect, the executor *shall not* change the marking and *shall not* move its loop to another step: the tokens that the firings in flight consumed stay consumed ([EXEC-031]), and the current cycle goes on.
The executor *shall* become stopped only when `terminateNow()` takes effect, and once stopped it *shall* stay stopped; `close()` *shall not* stop it ([ENV-013]).
*While* the executor is stopped, *if* `inject()` is called, *then* it *shall* return an error or `false` ([ENV-006]).
*While* the executor is stopped, it *shall not* inject an external event into the marking.
*While* the executor is stopped, it *shall not* process the outcome of a firing, except in the firing pass of the current cycle, for a synchronous action that pass waits for ([EXEC-001]).

*While* the executor is stopped and its loop is at the start of a cycle, it *shall not* take any step of the loop other than ending the run (answering a snapshot request ([ENV-014]) is not a step of the loop).
*When* the executor is stopped and its loop reaches the start of a cycle, it *shall* end the run without waiting for the actions still in flight.

*When* the executor ends a run because it is stopped, it *shall* end it at the start of a cycle, *shall* return the marking it holds at that point without restoring the tokens that the firings in flight consumed, and *shall* discard every external event still queued ([ENV-004]).
*While* the executor is stopped, it *shall not* deposit a batch that an action published mid-action ([IO-015]), except to finish a step 1b that was under way when the call took effect.

*While* the executor is stopped, it *shall not* end the firing pass of the current cycle while transitions remain in its ready order: the pass still starts each of them that it can start ([EXEC-002], [TIME-014]).
Which termination reason the run reports is [EXEC-041]'s.
Whether an action left running is cancelled is the runtime's capability ([IO-013]); the executor never deposits its result.
assumes: The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. A call of terminateNow() is the outside step terminateNow, and 'the executor is stopped' is the lifecycle mode Mode.stopped (ruling D47 (c)). The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean): terminateStep sets the mode stopped, keeps the phase, empties the event queue (Java completes the queued events with false inside terminateNow) and clears the parked flag, which ends the wait; settleOk refuses step 1 and the wait once stopped and lets the pass settle only a synchronous firing, publishStep refuses a stopped wait, endPass needs an empty order, endCompletions refuses a stopped state, and finish stopped is offered at phase completions.

Naming: 'takes effect' is the terminateNow step, which sits between two steps of the loop. Java sets its flags at the call and reads stopRequested at the top of its loop (BitmapNetExecutor.executeLoop), so a call that lands during step 1 lets Java finish that step and the rest of the cycle; the model reads such a call as taking effect at the end of the step under way. A request that lands between the call and that point is, in the model, accepted and then dropped by the terminateNow step, which the quoted sentence 'A request that lands before the call takes effect may still be accepted; ...' allows: Java refuses it at once, and the caller learns false either way (ENV-004 reads the terminateNow step as the false answer of every ticket it drops). 'The start of a cycle' is the phase completions (EXEC-001 step 1, entered by endPass after a pass that started a transition, by wake, or by a settle in the wait); the current cycle ends where the next would start. 'The firing pass of the current cycle' is the phase pass: once stopped, line 7 lets no later cycle get past its start, so the only pass a stopped executor is in is the current cycle's. 'A synchronous action that pass waits for' is a firing in flight whose sync flag is set (the pass waits for it, passFree). 'Move its loop to another step' is a change of phase; 'end a wait under way' is clearing the parked flag. 'Step 1b' is the phase publications. 'Process the outcome of a firing' is a settle step (commit, fail, tdeposit, EXEC-020, EXEC-030, EXEC-022). 'Ends a run because it is stopped' is finish stopped. 'Ending the run' in line 7 is any finish: the quoted reason sentence leaves the reason to EXEC-041 (ruling D53 (c): closed and quiescent also conform after an immediate termination), and a terminal place stops the run from any phase (EXEC-042).

Lines 1 and 2 are the shall sentence 'The executor shall become stopped only when terminateNow() takes effect, and once stopped it shall stay stopped; close() shall not stop it' and 'It is an explicit escape hatch and MUST NOT be invoked implicitly by close()'. They pin what EXEC-041's lines 6 and 7 read as 'an immediate termination was requested': the mode of the source state. A close that terminates immediately breaks line 1 (ENV_015_forbids_closeAsStop); a close after the stop that reopens a lifecycle that admits completions breaks line 2 (ENV_015_forbids_closeAfterStop; Java's close() after terminateNow() only sets flags that are already set). That a close itself changes only the mode to closed is ENV-013's line 1.

Line 3 is the two shall sentences on the moment terminateNow() takes effect, item 2 ('Queued external events are discarded') and item 4's 'their consumed tokens are lost'. A stop written as a close, which waits for the actions in flight and admits their completions, breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_terminateAsClose), and so does a stop that puts back the tokens the firings in flight consumed (ENV_015_forbids_rollbackAtTerminate). The phase conjunct is 'shall not move its loop to another step' and item 3's 'The loop stops at the end of its current cycle': a stop that ends the run at the call (Java's terminateNow() completing the run future itself) breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_endsAtCall), and so would a stop that jumps to the start of the next cycle. The queue conjunct is 'shall discard every external event still queued': a stop that keeps the queue and drops it later, in step 2 or at the finish, breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_queueKeptAtStop). The parked conjunct is 'shall end a wait under way in step 6': a stop that leaves a parked loop parked breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_stopKeepsWait). A second terminateNow() of a stopped executor is no step of the reference (Java's second call sets flags already set); line 3 does not need it.

Line 4 is item 1 and the shall sentence on inject(): a stopped executor answers refused (false) or error, never accepted (ENV_015_forbids_acceptWhileStopped). That a refused request changes nothing is ENV-006's. AC3's 'does not hang' is coverage: the third clause of Env015Covers (a request to a stopped executor is answered), which the reference meets (env015_ref_covers).

Line 5 is item 2 and the shall sentence on injection: no queued event reaches the marking once the executor is stopped. An executor that keeps the queue at the stop and injects what was sent before it (the Rust reading of a close, ENV-013, carried over to the stop) breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_injectWhileStopped). The reference drops the queue at the stop, and line 8 drops what is left at the finish; the admission signal of every dropped event completes with false (ENV-004).

Line 6 is item 3's 'their results are discarded rather than admitted to the marking' and its shall sentence: once stopped, no outcome is processed in step 1 or in the wait (EXEC-001), so a late return is never committed or failed. The firing pass of the current cycle is part of that cycle: a synchronous action it waits for still completes inside it (Java runs it inline on the orchestrator thread and deposits its output there; the Java test that calls terminateNow() from inside an action), and ENV_015_nonvacuous commits such a firing in a stopped pass. The exemption is the synchronous firing only: an asynchronous firing whose outcome is queued when the pass is under way is not settled there (settleOk), so an executor that admits a late completion in the wait (ENV_015_forbids_lateAdmit) or that commits an asynchronous firing's queued outcome in a stopped pass (ENV_015_forbids_asyncInPass) breaks the line.

Line 7 is item 3's 'The loop stops at the end of its current cycle' and its shall sentence: at the start of a cycle a stopped executor ends the run and goes no further. An executor that runs on into another cycle once stopped breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_goesOn). Answers to a snapshot request are exempt, as the sentence's parenthesis and EXEC-041's naming say: a snapshot answer reads the state and is not a step of the loop, and what it answers is ENV-014's (the reference offers none at phase completions).

The shall sentence 'When the executor is stopped and its loop reaches the start of a cycle, it shall end the run without waiting for the actions still in flight' and item 3's 'it does NOT wait for in-flight actions' say that the end of the run is offered at once, firings in flight or not (AC1). That is coverage, which a safety line cannot state: Env015Covers below is the conjunct for the consistency theorem, a clause of ExecCoversW5 (ConsistencyExec.lean) (finish stopped offered at a live stopped start of a cycle, wake offered in a live stopped wait, a request answered). An executor whose stop waits for every action in flight to return (env015_wait, the stop written in the shape of a close) meets every line (env015_wait_meets) and fails the conjunct (env015_wait_not_covered). The wait the stop ends: line 3 clears the parked flag, and the second clause offers the wake; the reference still offers a park after the stop (parkStep has no mode guard), which with the wake that follows is a stutter, and 'does not wait' rests on the wake being offered.

Line 8 is the last shall sentence: finish stopped happens at the start of a cycle, not in the middle of one (ENV_015_forbids_stopMidCycle), keeps the marking, so the tokens the abandoned firings consumed stay consumed (ENV_015_forbids_rollbackOnStop; EXEC-041 line 1 also keeps the marking at every finish), and drops the queued events (ENV_015_forbids_keepQueued: an executor that keeps them queued past the end never answers them).

Item 4's 'In-flight actions keep running where the runtime cannot cancel them ([IO-013])': no line requires the firings in flight to stay in the list of firings, since a runtime that can cancel an action may; the reference keeps them (finish stopped keeps fl), and their outside steps go on after the finish (ENV_015_nonvacuous returns t's action after the finish). That nothing such a late result does changes the returned marking is EXEC-041's lines 2 and 3; whether the action is stopped is IO-013's.

Termination reason: the reference reports stopped. Java reports CLOSED after terminateNow(), because terminateNow() also sets the closed flag, and the reason chain in executeLoop's finally reads closed before STOPPED; EXEC-041 allows closed after an immediate termination. Java's CLOSED with an action still in flight matches no reference finish closed (which needs nothing in flight); that is the reason's question (EXEC-041, ENV-013), not this block's: the sentence 'Which termination reason the run reports is [EXEC-041]'s.' says so.

Line 9 is the shall sentence on mid-action publications (IO-015, step 1b) and the sentence 'the executor never deposits its result': once stopped, no flushed batch lands in the wait or anywhere outside step 1b. A step 1b under way when the call took effect still finishes (the call takes effect when that step ends), which the reference allows at phase publications; a stopped executor reaches that phase only that way, since line 7 holds it at the start of a cycle. A Rust or Python wait whose flush arm deposits unconditionally, given a stop flag read at the top of the loop as Java reads it, breaks the line (ENV_015_forbids_publishWhileStopped: the batch t flushed lands on the wake the stop caused, and the run ends stopped with 70 in place 1). Publications are a Rust and Python feature, and only Java has terminateNow(); the line binds a runtime that has both.

Line 10 is the shall sentence on the firing pass of the current cycle: the stop does not cut the pass short, so the transitions left in its ready order are still offered, each started or lost as EXEC-002 and TIME-014 say (whether a head can start is theirs). An executor whose pass breaks off at the stop (an early exit in Java's fireReadyTransitions or the TypeScript firing loop) breaks it (ENV_015_forbids_passBreaksOff: stopped with t at the head of the order, the pass ends without starting t, and the run then ends with 7 still in place 0). ENV_015_nonvacuous starts t in a stopped pass.
Scope: the Status is Proposed and the operation is a MAY. Rust, TypeScript and Python take no terminateNow step, so lines 3 to 8 say nothing about them, and line 1 holds of them (no step stops them).

AC1 (terminateNow() stops the loop without awaiting an outstanding in-flight action) is lines 3, 6, 7 and 8 with the coverage conjunct; ENV_015_nonvacuous takes terminateNow with t's action in flight, offers no endCompletions at the next start of a cycle and finishes stopped with t still in flight.

AC2 (the in-flight action's eventual output is not admitted to the marking) is lines 6 and 9, with EXEC-041's lines 2 and 3 after the finish; ENV_015_nonvacuous offers no commit of t's returned output in a stopped wait or a stopped pass, no publication of its flushed batch in a stopped wait, and t's return after the finish leaves place 1 empty.

AC3 (inject() after terminateNow() returns error / false, does not hang) is line 4 with the third coverage clause; ENV_015_nonvacuous answers a request for the environment place refused and one for another place error, and offers no accepted answer. A call made after terminateNow() returns but before the call takes effect is the quoted sentence on a request that lands before the call takes effect: its answer may be accepted, and its admission completes with false (line 3 and ENV-004).

The test derivation (a gated in-flight action, terminateNow(), the loop ends without releasing the gate, the output never reaches the marking) is ENV_015_nonvacuous's run: t starts asynchronously, the executor stops, finishes stopped, and t's later return deposits nothing.

requirements.title: Observable Termination
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R X ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (on fun s s' ↦ X C TimeoutPolicy.abandon s s', shall fun s s' ↦ s' = s) ∧
      (on fun s s' ↦ X C TimeoutPolicy.close s s', shall fun s s' ↦
          (s.mode = Mode.open ∨ s.mode = Mode.draining → R C s XLbl.close s') ∧
            (s.mode = Mode.closed ∨ s.mode = Mode.stopped → s' = s)) ∧
        ∀ (pol : TimeoutPolicy),
          on fun s s' ↦ X C pol s s' ∧ isExecPhase s.phase = true, shall fun s s' ↦
            isExecPhase s'.phase = true ∧ s'.M = s.M
requirements.scope: executors that provide run-with-timeout with a timeout policy (Java, TypeScript)
reading: For every executor R, every expiry handling X of its run-with-timeout and every configuration C:
an expiry under abandon from state s ends in s itself;
an expiry under close from a state s whose mode is open or draining ends in a state that a close step of R reaches from s, and from a state s whose mode is closed or stopped it ends in s itself;
an expiry from a state in which the loop is running ends in a state in which the loop is still running, with the same marking.
quotes: Independently, run-with-timeout (`run(timeout)`, whose timeout is the caller's run budget named in [EXEC-041]; its expiry fails the caller's wait and does not by itself end the run) MAY expose a policy for what happens to the loop when the caller's timeout expires: *abandon* (leave the loop running; the historical default, rarely desirable) or *close* (stop it per [ENV-013]).
The expiry of the caller's timeout MUST NOT complete the loop's own result: an abandoned loop can still report its real final marking.
*Where* an implementation exposes this policy, *when* the caller's timeout expires while the loop is running, the implementation *shall* act on the expiry under the policy the caller chose.

*When* the caller's timeout expires under *abandon*, the implementation *shall* leave the executor as it was, including its marking, its lifecycle mode, its queues, its firings in flight and the position of its loop, and a running loop *shall* go on running.

*When* the caller's timeout expires under *close* while the executor is open or draining, the implementation *shall* close the executor as a call of `close()` does ([ENV-013]), even while its loop is running.
*When* the caller's timeout expires under *close* after the executor is already closed or stopped, the implementation *shall* leave the executor as it was.
*When* the caller's timeout expires while the loop is running, the implementation *shall not* end the run and *shall not* change the marking.
Under a *close* policy the executor is closed on timeout and the loop then stops as [ENV-013] says, once its in-flight actions complete; under *abandon* it keeps running.
assumes: The model is a pair: an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean), where R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s', and the expiry handling X : ExpiryRel N T of its run-with-timeout, where X C pol s s' says that the expiry of the caller's timeout under policy pol (TimeoutPolicy: abandon or close) takes the executor from s to s'. The expiry is an event of the host's clock, which the model does not carry (ruling D18 (b)), so it is a relation beside R and not a label of XLbl. The caller's own result (Java's returned stage failing with a TimeoutException, TypeScript's rejected promise) is not executor state and is outside the model. The witnesses are the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean) and refExpiry: abandon changes nothing, close is RefExec's close step, or nothing when the executor is already closed or stopped.

That the expiry is handled under the policy the caller chose, and not another, is the meaning of X's policy argument: X C pol s s' is the handling of a run whose caller chose pol, so lines 1 and 2 say what each choice does, and the coverage clause Env016Covers says that the handling takes effect at all. The binding of the caller's argument to pol is not modelled further; an implementation that swapped the two policies breaks line 1 on the abandon side (ENV_016_forbids_abandonCloses) and line 2 on the close side (ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored).

Scope (Status Proposed, priority MAY, ruling D47 (c)): the block applies to the implementations that expose the policy, Java (run(Duration, RunTimeoutPolicy) in BitmapNetExecutor and PrecompiledNetExecutor) and TypeScript (run(timeoutMs, onTimeout) in both executors). Rust and Python have no run-with-timeout policy. Java's PetriNetExecutor interface has a default run(timeout, policy) that ignores the policy and abandons: an executor that keeps that default does not provide the close policy, and one that claimed to would break line 2 (ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored).

Its offer is in ExecCoversW5.Env016Covers (ConsistencyExec.lean; the convention of GlossaryExec.lean: offers are coverage clauses, never block lines). The third EARS sentence demands an answer and is quoted whole; its safety halves are lines 1 and 2, and its existence half is that clause: from every state in which the loop is running, an expiry under either policy has an outcome in X, which the reference meets (env016_ref_covers). AC3 is lines 1 to 3 with that clause. Under abandon the expiry changes nothing and the loop keeps running (line 1; ENV_016_forbids_abandonCloses: an expiry that closes the executor under abandon breaks it). Under close, from an open or draining executor, the expiry is the executor's own close step (line 2; ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored: an expiry that leaves the executor open breaks it, and so does ENV_016_forbids_closeTerminates, an expiry that stops the loop without waiting for its firings in flight, as terminateNow does under ENV-015). Line 2 reads 'already closed or stopped' on the lifecycle mode, not on the steps R offers, so line 2 and Env016Covers together require R to have a close step from every open or draining state in which its loop runs: an executor that refuses close() while its loop runs, so that the close policy acts as abandon, breaks line 2 (ENV_016_forbids_closeRefusedWhileRunning), and an expiry handling that gave such an executor no outcome there instead would fail Env016Covers. The expiry under close does not stop the loop at once (line 3; ENV_016_forbids_closeFinishes). That the loop then stops once its in-flight actions complete is ENV-013's requirement (its item 4), not a line of this block; ENV_016_nonvacuous part 3 shows it on the test derivation's run. Env016Covers makes the expiry take effect at all: an implementation whose expiry handler never runs meets every line and fails the clause (env016_covers_unhandled). The clause asks for an outcome only while the loop runs: once the run has returned, Java's orTimeout and TypeScript's cleared timer no longer fire.

The MUST NOT sentence is line 3 with line 1: no expiry while the loop runs ends the run or changes the marking, so the result the loop reports, the marking at its finish and the fact that it ended (EXEC-041), is fixed only by a finish step of the loop. Line 3 adds to line 1 only under close, where it constrains R's own close step; under abandon it follows from line 1. An implementation whose timer completes the loop's own result with the marking at the expiry, the defect Java's loop.copy() avoids, breaks line 1 (ENV_016_forbids_expiryCompletes); one whose close finishes the run at once, reporting the marking at the expiry, breaks line 3 although its expiry is its own close step (ENV_016_forbids_closeFinishes). 'An abandoned loop can still report its real final marking' is ENV_016_nonvacuous part 2: after an expiry under abandon the action in flight returns, its output is deposited, and the loop finishes quiescent with that output in the marking it reports.

The termination reason an abandoned run reports is EXEC-041's question, not this block's (env-b ENVB-R6 (a), ruling D53 (c)): TypeScript sets its reason to stopped when the caller's timeout expires and keeps it if the loop later ends on its own. That field is reporting state outside the executor state of the model, and D53 (c) allows it, since stopped is not a completed reason. Lines 1 and 3 speak of the executor state and the marking only.

Java closes the executor from a callback that runs after the returned stage has failed (whenCompleteAsync), so loop steps may come between the expiry and the close. The model places the expiry at the moment close() takes effect; a run in which loop steps come first is a run of R whose close step comes later. TypeScript calls close() in the turn that rejects the promise.

Which policy is the default is configuration (kind N) and not a line: run(timeout) without a policy abandons in Java and TypeScript, the historical default of the text. The lines hold for whichever policy the caller chooses.

Deferred to wave W7 (ruling D47 (c), plan W7): AC1, AC2 and the first paragraph, awaitTermination answering false while the loop runs and true once it has stopped and finished its termination bookkeeping (pending inject() futures completed, ExecutionCompleted emitted), returning promptly when the loop was never started, and not being defeated by a failure in that bookkeeping such as a throwing event store. Its answer depends on the emission of ExecutionCompleted, which needs the event model RefEvents; that line will join this block. Blocking, the timeout of awaitTermination and 'promptly' are kind Q.

The test derivation (a net with an action still in flight when a short timeout expires, under each policy; the executor closed under close and the loop stopping once the action completes, the loop still live under abandon and reporting the action's output) is ENV_016_nonvacuous: at the expiry the loop is still running, parked with a firing in flight; under close the executor is closed by R's close step and the loop finishes closed after the action completes; under abandon the executor is unchanged and the loop goes on to finish quiescent with the action's output. The awaitTermination half of the test derivation is W7's.

requirements.title: EventStore Interface
requirements.statement:
fun {E} S ↦
  ∀ (h h' : List (StoreOp E)),
    (List.map S.norm (S.read h h')).Sublist (List.map S.norm (appended (h ++ h')))
requirements.scope: every event store (the interface: the in-memory, noop, logging, debug and debug-aware stores of Java, TypeScript and Rust, and the Python binding's store)
reading: For every store S over any event type E, with S.norm the store's own normalisation of an event:

after every history h of appends and clears, the list a call of events() returns, as it shows once any further operations h' have run (S.read h h', the call itself being h' = []), read through S.norm, is a sublist of the events h and h' appended, in append order (appended (h ++ h')), read through S.norm.
quotes: The list `events()` returns *shall* be a subsequence of the events appended to the store: only appended events, in the order they were appended, each append at most once.
A store that keeps token payloads only for some places (the Python binding's `capture_tokens` filter) is compared with the appended events after the same payloads are removed from them.
Which appended events the list leaves out, and whether it is a copy or a live view of the store, is up to each store ([EVT-021], [EVT-022], [EVT-024]).
assumes: The normalisation S.norm is part of the store's observation and is the one the store applies, not one chosen to meet the line (glossary: StoreObs.norm, the identity unless a store says otherwise): it is the identity for every store but the Python binding's in-memory store, so for them the line is the subsequence law itself (evt020_id_iff), and for the binding's store it is the store's capture-filter strip (see below). A normalisation the store does not apply is no reading of the block: read through a constant, every store would meet the line.

The model is the observation of one store, S : StoreObs E (glossary: Event store): its enabled flag, whether it provides clear(), and read h h', the list a call of events() made after the history h shows once the further operations h' have run. The event type E is a parameter: the line says nothing about what an event holds. The first quoted sentence is the line, at the call (h' = []) and at every later point. The second is why the line compares with every append so far (appended (h ++ h')) and not only with the appends before the call: ruling D29 (a) leaves open whether the list is a copy (Java's List.copyOf, the Python binding's new list; Rust lends a borrow that no append can change while it is held) or a live view (TypeScript's in-memory and debug stores return their own array), and both meet the line (EVT_020_reference, EVT_020_bounded, evt020_allows_live, evt020_allows_liveBounded). What the line asks of a live view is that it stays a view of the store, a subsequence of the appends in append order at every later point; a bounded store that hands out its raw ring buffer breaks that (EVT_020_mutant_ringView), and evt020_atCall gives the reading at the call alone.

AC2 (events() returns a subsequence of the appended events, in append order; whether that list is a copy or a live view is not specified) is the line, under ruling D29 (a), which words the body bullet and AC2 so (clash evt-b#6): the noop store returns no event (EVT-022) and the bounded debug stores evict the oldest (EVT-024). That the in-memory store returns every event appended since the last clear, as a copy, is EVT-021's.

The line compares with every append of the history, clears ignored, so it says nothing about what clear() does: a store whose clear() keeps every event meets it (evt020_allows_keepAcrossClear). What a store shows after clear(), where it provides clear() (ruling D29 (a)), is EVT-021's.

AC3 (isEnabled() controls whether the executor appends events to the store) and the body sentence that an executor appends events to a store only while the store reports itself as enabled are the glossary fact storeSink, not a line of this block (design events.md SC-8): what an executor appends to a store is storeSink S tr, every emitted event when S reports itself enabled and nothing otherwise. The markdown words that sentence as a statement of how events reach a store and not as a shall, since no store and no executor model can fail a definition. The flag constrains the executor and not the store: a store that reports itself not enabled and keeps what a caller appends to it directly meets the line (evt020_allows_disabledKeeps), and evt020_sink_disabled shows that a store meeting the line which reports itself not enabled shows nothing an executor emitted. The executor blocks of wave W7 emit through storeSink. Whether an executor builds the event objects of a disabled store at all is kind Q (clash evt-b#12, PERF-010 and ruling D34, EVT-022 AC4): TypeScript and the Java bitmap executor build them and test the flag only when appending.

The enabled flag is a constant of the store for a whole run (clash evt-b#11): TypeScript reads isEnabled() once when the executor is built, Java when it is built and again at every emit, Rust fixes it at compile time as the store type's ENABLED constant. A store whose isEnabled() answer changes during a run is outside the model.

AC1 (append() is safe to call from any thread) is kind A and has no line, although the requirement as a whole is kind F: a history is one sequence of operations, and appends made at once from several threads are read in the order in which they take effect (Java's in-memory and debug stores append to a ConcurrentLinkedQueue). The obligation has content in Java only, where captured logs and ActionTimedOut are appended from threads other than the orchestrator's; in Rust append takes exclusive access (&mut self), TypeScript runs on one thread, and the Python binding's store appends under a mutex. That no concurrent append is lost is the in-memory store's promise (EVT-021 AC2), not this block's.

The three bullets of the body (append, events, isEnabled) name the operations: append is an operation of a history, events() is read, isEnabled() is the enabled flag. size() and isEmpty(), which the runtimes also offer, and the query helpers over events() (EVT-030) are not named by this block. Rust has no isEnabled() method; the store type's associated constant ENABLED plays its part (rust/libpetri-event/src/event_store.rs:19).

Decorators: Java's logging store (EVT-023) and the debug-aware stores of all three runtimes return the list of the store they wrap, so they meet the line whenever the wrapped store does and receives its appends only through the decorator (evt020_forward, which reads the decorator's history as the wrapped store's). Appends made directly to the wrapped store, by a caller that kept a reference to it, are outside the line: they show in the decorator's events() without having been appended to the decorator. Its events() called with filter, limit or offset arguments is a query (EVT-030); the call without them is the events() of this block. The Python run sink's own events() (the trait method) returns the empty list and is never called by the executor.

The Python binding's in-memory store strips the token payload of a TokenAdded or TokenRemoved event on a place outside its capture filter before keeping it (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs:350-367); the executor attaches that payload only because the store asks for payloads (its CAPTURES_TOKENS constant). For that store S.norm is the store's own strip, the normalisation that removes the payload of a token event on a place outside the store's capture filter (evt020_pyStrip), which is the second quoted sentence: evt020_allows_python shows the binding's store meets the line so read, at every capture filter, and evt020_python_inverted shows that a store whose strip is inverted (it removes the payloads inside the filter and keeps the others) does not. Read through the identity, the binding's store fails the line (evt020_python_literal), since it shows the stripped event, which the executor never appended. Which payloads the capture filter keeps is specified by no other requirement. A store meeting the line through the identity meets it through any normalisation (evt020_through_of).

The test derivation (append from several threads; events() returns only appended events, each at most once, in the order the appends took effect, and on the in-memory store all of them) is EVT_020_nonvacuous for the in-memory store: after appends whose order mixes two callers, events() returns all of them in that order, a live view of it still a subsequence after one more append, and the newest-first store fails the line on the same history. That the in-memory store returns every one of them is EVT-021's line, not this block's.

requirements.title: InMemoryEventStore
requirements.statement:
fun {E} S ↦
  S.read [] [] = [] ∧
    (∀ (h : List (StoreOp E)) (e : E),
        S.read (h ++ [StoreOp.append e]) [] = S.read h [] ++ [e]) ∧
      (S.hasClear = true →
          ∀ (h : List (StoreOp E)), S.read (h ++ [StoreOp.clear]) [] = []) ∧
        S.enabled = true
requirements.scope: the in-memory event store (Java EventStore.inMemory(), TypeScript InMemoryEventStore, Rust InMemoryEventStore, Python InMemoryEventStore)
reading: For every store S over any event type E:
after the empty history, a call of events() returns the empty list;
for every history h and event e, a call of events() after h followed by append e returns what a call after h returns, with e added at the end;
if S provides clear(), then for every history h a call of events() after h followed by clear returns the empty list;
S reports itself as enabled.
quotes: A new in-memory event store *shall* return no event from `events()`.

*When* an event is appended to the in-memory event store, a call of `events()` made right after the append *shall* return the events that a call made right before the append returns, with that event added at the end.
*Where* the in-memory event store provides `clear()`, a call of `events()` made right after `clear()` *shall* return no event.

The in-memory event store *shall* report itself as enabled, so that an executor appends every event it emits to it (see [EVT-020]): `isEnabled()` returns true in Java and TypeScript, the store type's `ENABLED` constant is true in Rust, and the Python binding's store is written through a Rust store whose `ENABLED` constant is true.
A call of `events()` changes nothing that a later call of `events()` returns, so the sentences above speak of what a call returns after the appends and clears made so far.
assumes: The model is the observation of one store, S : StoreObs E (glossary: Event store): its enabled flag, whether it provides clear(), and read h h', the list a call of events() made after the history h shows once the further operations h' have run. Every line reads h' = [] only, the list as returned, so the block says nothing about what a returned list shows after later operations (ruling D29 (a)). The event type E is a parameter: the lines say nothing about what an event holds.

The fifth quoted sentence is the premise of that model, not a line, and the markdown words it as a statement of what the observation assumes and not as a shall, as EVT-020 words the storeSink sentence: a history holds appends and clears only, so read h [] can stand for every call of events() after h only when a call changes nothing a later call returns, and no store in this model can fail it. Section 'Calls of events()' states it on histories that contain calls (evt021_CallFree): on a call-free store that meets the block, every call returns the events appended since the last clear (evt021_calls_retained), the reference is call-free (evt021_ref_callFree), and a store whose events() drains it (a poll() loop over Java's ConcurrentLinkedQueue in place of List.copyOf) meets the block on its first calls but is not call-free (evt021_drain_accepted, evt021_drain_not_callFree). Every runtime is call-free: Java returns List.copyOf, TypeScript returns its array, Rust's events() takes the store by shared reference, and the Python binding builds a new list under its mutex.

The body sentence (the store retains all events, in order) and AC1 (events are stored in insertion order) are lines 1 and 2 and the first two quoted sentences: by induction they give that a history of appends only is returned in full and in append order (evt021_appends), and with clear() that events() returns exactly the events appended since the last clear (evt021_read_retained). The order is append order: the body's earlier wording 'chronological order' is reworded to it under ruling D20 (clash evt-c#14), because event timestamps need not rise along the appends, and every runtime keeps the order of the appends (a ConcurrentLinkedQueue in Java, a pushed array in TypeScript, a pushed Vec in Rust and in the Python binding). A store that orders its events by timestamp (evt021_chronoStore) violates line 2.

AC2 (thread-safe append, concurrent callers do not lose events) is kind Q: a history is one linear order of operations, so no line can show a lost concurrent append. It matters in Java, whose store appends lock-free to a ConcurrentLinkedQueue from the orchestrator, action and timeout threads (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/event/EventStore.java:252-273); Rust's append takes the store mutably and the Python binding locks a mutex around it (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs), and TypeScript runs on one thread. What line 2 does show is that no append, concurrent or not, is lost once it has run.

AC3 (events() returns the events appended since the last clear(), in append order; what a returned list shows after later operations is not specified) is lines 1 and 2 for the events it returns, through evt021_read_retained and evt021_appends. What a returned list shows later is not a line: ruling D29 (a) leaves the copy unspecified, because TypeScript's store returns its own array, which grows on later appends (typescript/src/event/event-store.ts:58-60; clash evt-c#1), while Java returns List.copyOf, Rust lends a borrowed slice that the borrow checker keeps from changing while it is held, and Python builds a new list. The block accepts every such later view, not only a copy or a live view: EVT_021_allows_live shows the live-array store, and EVT_021_allows_detached a TypeScript store whose clear() replaces its array, so a list returned earlier stops following the store. The spec edit of this wave rewords AC3 from 'a snapshot copy (not a live reference)' to that ruling.

AC4 (clear() for test reuse) is line 3 and the third quoted sentence, under ruling D29 (a): clear() is required only where the store provides it, and the spec edit of this wave rewords AC4 to say so. hasClear is read off the store's class, not off the type a factory returns: it is true for TypeScript's InMemoryEventStore and for Java's package-private InMemoryEventStore, whose public clear() is callable from its own package although EventStore.inMemory() returns it as the EventStore interface (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/event/EventStore.java:195, :252, :271), and false for Rust's and the Python binding's stores, which have none (rust/libpetri-event/src/event_store.rs:67-86; python/libpetri/_libpetri.pyi; clash evt-c#2). So a Java clear() that does nothing is the store EVT_021_mutant_ignoreClear rejects. EVT_021_allows_noClear shows the store without clear() meets the block. A history with a clear made on a store without clear() is not one a caller can make; line 2 quantifies over every history and covers it anyway, which every runtime meets.

Line 4 and the fourth quoted sentence are a new sentence derived from 'retains all events' and stated with that derivation: an executor appends to a store only when it reports itself enabled (the glossary's storeSink, EVT-020 AC3, 'isEnabled() controls whether the executor appends events to the store'), so a store that keeps every append but reports itself not enabled would retain none of a run's events. All runtimes meet it: Java's in-memory store keeps the interface default isEnabled() = true, TypeScript's returns true, Rust's sets ENABLED = true, and the executor writes the Python binding's store through a Rust store whose ENABLED is true (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs, RunStore). evt021_sink states the consequence: every event an executor emits reaches a store that meets the block, in emission order.

Scope: the line is on the in-memory store, not on every store that keeps events. The bounded debug stores evict their oldest events (EVT-024) and violate line 2 (EVT_021_forbids_bounded); the noop store (EVT-022) violates lines 2 and 4 (EVT_021_forbids_noop), so no one store meets both blocks (evt021_not_noop) and the consistency theorem gives each its own store variable. The query helpers the runtimes offer on the store (filter, transitionEvents, failures, and the Python filters, limit and offset) are EVT-030's; size(), isEmpty() and len() are not named by the spec and not modelled.
The test derivation (append 100 events; events() returns 100 in order) is EVT_021_nonvacuous on the reference, which also shows the last-in-first-out store returning the same appends reversed.

requirements.title: NoopEventStore
requirements.statement: fun {E} S ↦ (∀ (h h' : List (StoreOp E)), S.read h h' = []) ∧ S.enabled = false
requirements.scope: the noop event store (Java EventStore.noop(), TypeScript noopEventStore(), Rust NoopEventStore)
reading: For every store S over any event type E:
after every history h of appends and clears, a call of events() returns the empty list, and the list it returned still shows nothing after any further operations h';
S reports itself as not enabled.
quotes: The noop event store *shall* return no event from `events()`, whatever was appended to it, and the list it returns *shall* stay empty whatever is appended to it later.
*When* an event is appended to the noop event store, the store *shall* discard it.
The noop event store *shall* report itself as not enabled (`isEnabled()` returns false; in Rust, the store type's `ENABLED` constant is false).
assumes: The model is the observation of one store, S : StoreObs E (glossary: Event store): its enabled flag, whether it provides clear(), and read h h', the list a call of events() made after the history h shows once the further operations h' have run. The event type E is a parameter: the line says nothing about what an event holds. The first quoted sentence is line 1; its second half ('stays empty') is the quantifier over h', which all three runtimes meet with an immutable empty list (Java List.of(), a frozen empty array in TypeScript, the static empty slice in Rust).

The second quoted sentence (AC1, append() is a no-op) is read as line 1: a store's append is observed only through events(), so an append that no later call of events() shows is discarded. evt022_append_noop states it as a consequence: removing an append from any history changes nothing a call of events() shows. size() and isEmpty(), which the runtimes also offer, are not named by the spec and not modelled.

AC2 (events() returns empty) is line 1. AC3 (isEnabled() returns false) is line 2 and the third quoted sentence; Rust has no isEnabled() method, and its noop store type sets the associated constant ENABLED to false, which the executor reads at compile time (rust/libpetri-event/src/event_store.rs:39-59).

AC4 (the executor does not allocate event objects when the noop store is used) and the body sentence 'When used, the executor skips event object creation entirely' are kind Q: allocation is not observable in a model of what a store shows, and PERF-010's benchmark is their test. They are false of both TypeScript executors and of the Java bitmap executor, which build event objects and test the enabled flag only when appending (clash perf#4); ruling D34 (a) rewords them in wave W11 to what every runtime meets. The observable half, that an executor appends nothing to a store that reports itself not enabled, is EVT-020's AC3 and is not restated here: the glossary's storeSink decides it from the enabled flag, and evt022_sink shows it gives a store that meets this block nothing.

Clear: none of the three noop stores provides clear() (ruling D29 (a): clear() where provided), so a history with a clear is not one a caller can make; line 1 quantifies over every history and covers it anyway.

Scope: the line is on the noop store, not on every store that discards. Java's EventStore.logging() wraps the noop store in the logging decorator (EVT-023), which discards every event but reports itself enabled, so an executor builds and hands it every event; it is a different store and is the mutant evt022_discardEnabled here, not a runtime that fails the block. The debug-aware store over the noop store has the same shape in all three runtimes (enabled, events() empty) and is outside the line for the same reason.

Python has no noop store object: a run given no event store, or a store whose is_enabled is false, runs on Rust's NoopEventStore (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs, RunSink::Noop), so the Rust store covers it.
The test derivation is EVT_022_nonvacuous for its first half (a history of appends leaves events() empty while the in-memory store shows the same appends); its benchmark half is AC4's.

requirements.title: LoggingEventStore
requirements.statement:
fun {E} kind D ↦
  (∀ (W : StoreObs E) (th : LogLevel) (e : E),
      observed th (D.onAppend W th e) =
        observed th [LogEffect.log (eventLogLevel (kind e)) e, LogEffect.pass e]) ∧
    (∀ (W : StoreObs E) (h h' : List (StoreOp E)), (D.over W).read h h' = W.read h h') ∧
      ∀ (W : StoreObs E), (D.over W).enabled = true
requirements.scope: the logging event store decorator (Java EventStore.logging() and EventStore.logging(delegate)); TypeScript, Rust and Python have none
reading: For every event type E with its kind function kind : E → NetEventKind, and every logging decorator D over E:

for every wrapped store W, every framework threshold th and every event e, the effects of an append of e that a caller observes with the framework at th (the log calls at a level th enables, which are the records the framework writes, and every pass) are those of one log call for e at the level eventLogLevel (kind e) followed by one pass of e to the wrapped store, and no other; the table eventLogLevel gives WARN to the three failure kinds, INFO to ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted, DEBUG to the other four transition kinds, and TRACE to TokenAdded, TokenRemoved, MarkingSnapshot and LogMessage;
for every wrapped store W and all histories h and h', a call of events() on D around W shows what a call of events() on W shows;
for every wrapped store W, D around W reports itself as enabled.
quotes: *When* an event is appended to the logging event store, the store *shall* log the event once, at the level of the event's kind, *shall* then pass the event once to the wrapped store, and *shall* log no other record and pass no other event, whatever store it wraps.
The logging event store *shall* make the logging call of an event whenever the logging framework has the call's level enabled, and *may* skip the call when the framework has that level disabled.
The logging event store *shall* log TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut events at WARN level.
The logging event store *shall* log ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted events at INFO level.
The logging event store *shall* log TransitionEnabled, TransitionClockRestarted, TransitionStarted and TransitionCompleted events at DEBUG level.
The logging event store *shall* log TokenAdded, TokenRemoved, MarkingSnapshot and LogMessage events at TRACE level.
The logging event store *shall* return from `events()` what the wrapped store returns.
The logging event store *shall* report itself as enabled, whatever the wrapped store reports (`isEnabled()` returns true).
assumes: The model is the observation of one decorator, D : LogDecorator E: onAppend W th e, the effects of one append(e) on the decorator around the store W with the logging framework at the threshold th, in order (a log call at a level, or passing an event to the wrapped store), and over W, the decorator around W observed as a store (glossary: Event store). The event type E is a parameter and is read only through kind : E → NetEventKind, so the block says nothing about an event's payload or about the text of a log message (Java logs the transition name, token counts and durations; a message format is not a line). The kind function is the event model's (wave W7's glossary of events: the kind of each of the thirteen events of EVT-002 to EVT-014), not a choice of the implementation: a decorator paired with a kind function that maps every event to TokenAdded would log everything at TRACE and meet the line, so the line binds only with the event model's kind function, and tying the two is an obligation of the W7 integrator, recorded in the consistency module of the events (ConsistencyEvents.lean).

The configuration of the logging framework is a threshold th: a level is enabled when it is th or more severe (LogLevel.loggableAt; System.Logger levels are ordered, and its default backend, java.util.logging, filters by a threshold). A log call at a disabled level writes no record, so line 1 compares the observed effects only, and a decorator may make or skip such a call, as the second quoted sentence says. Java skips it: logEvent returns early when DEBUG is not loggable and the event is not a WARN or INFO kind (EventStore.java:370, 418-425), and refLogStore has that guard. EVT_023_mutant_slipGuard is the guard with ActionTimedOut left out: with every level enabled it logs as Java does, but with the framework at INFO it writes no WARN record for an ActionTimedOut, so it violates line 1. A framework filter that is not a threshold, and a logging call that throws, are out of scope.

Line 1 is the first six quoted sentences. The first fixes the two effects, their order, that there is no other, and that they do not depend on the wrapped store: onAppend is given W, and line 1 holds for every W. EVT_023_mutant_logTwice and EVT_023_mutant_passTwice keep the order and log or pass a second time, so they violate 'once'. EVT_023_mutant_gatedOnWrapped logs and passes nothing around a store that reports itself not enabled, as an append guarded by the wrapped store's isEnabled() would, so EventStore.logging() would log nothing; it meets line 1 around the in-memory store and violates it around the noop store. The second sentence is the threshold. The other four are the level table eventLogLevel, which names each of the thirteen kinds once.

AC1, AC2, AC3 and AC4 (failure events at WARN, lifecycle events at INFO, the other transition events at DEBUG, token events, MarkingSnapshot and LogMessage at TRACE) are the table of line 1. As first written they overlapped and did not cover every kind: TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut are both failure and transition events, and MarkingSnapshot and LogMessage were in no class (clash evt-c#3). Ruling D29 (a) (evt-c EVT-C3 (a)) writes Java's table into the requirement, failures first, and the spec edit of this wave names the kinds in each AC. EVT_023_mutant_transitionFirst is AC3 read literally (TransitionFailed at DEBUG) and violates line 1. eventLogLevel_failure states that every failure kind, the set EVT-030's failures() returns, is logged at WARN.

AC5 (delegates to the wrapped store after logging) is the order in line 1 and line 2. evt023_passedOn states the consequence that the wrapped store receives exactly the events appended to the decorator, in order, so line 2 compares the decorator and W after the same history; with line 2 the decorator holds no list of its own (Java's events(), size() and isEmpty() call the delegate). The clause of AC5 on events() and the sixth quoted sentence were added under ruling D20: they restate what Java, the only implementation, does. size() and isEmpty() are not named by the spec and not modelled. Line 2 quantifies over every history, clears included, so a clear() the decorator provided would have to leave events() as a clear on the wrapped store does; Java's decorator provides none, and the block does not constrain hasClear.

AC6 (reports itself as enabled whatever store it wraps) is line 3 and the last quoted sentence, both added under ruling D20 as what Java does. It is what makes EventStore.logging(), the decorator around the noop store, log anything: an executor appends only to a store that reports itself enabled (the glossary's storeSink, EVT-020 AC3), so a decorator that reported the noop store's flag would receive no event. Java's LoggingEventStore.isEnabled() returns true (EventStore.java:355-358; LoggingEventStoreTest.shouldAlwaysBeEnabled). evt023_sink states the consequence; evt023_not_noop shows that the decorator around any store is not a noop store, which is EVT-022's mutant evt022_discardEnabled.

Scope: Java only. TypeScript, Rust and the Python binding have no logging store, as the implementation notes say; the requirement is a SHOULD. The implementation note naming SLF4J is out of date: the class logs through java.lang.System.Logger (EventStore.java:336), and the spec edit of this wave corrects it and adds the missing Python line (ruling D20, evt-c EVT-C11 item 4).

The test derivation (run a net with the logging store and check the levels of the log output) is EVT_023_nonvacuous: the thirteen kinds appended through an executor's sink to the reference around the in-memory store give, with every level enabled, the log records at the table's levels in order, and with the framework at INFO only the WARN and INFO records; events() returns the thirteen events; the transition-first table gives other records.

requirements.title: DebugEventStore
requirements.statement:
fun {E} c S ↦
  ∀ (es : List E), S.read (List.map StoreOp.append es) [] = List.drop (es.length - c) es
requirements.scope: the debug event store (Java DebugEventStore, TypeScript DebugEventStore, Rust libpetri-debug DebugEventStore)
reading: For every capacity c and every store S over any event type E:

after a history of appends only, appending the events es one after the other, a call of events() returns the last c events of es (all of es when es has at most c events), in the order they were appended.
quotes: *When* events have been appended to a debug event store one after the other, a call of `events()` *shall* return the newest of them, as many as the store's capacity allows, in the order they were appended.
assumes: The model is the observation of one store, S : StoreObs E (glossary: Event store), and its capacity c, a parameter of the line: the line holds at every capacity, and EVT_024_reference shows the reference bounded store meets it at every capacity. The event type E is a parameter: the line says nothing about what an event holds. The line reads a call of events() at the call (h' = []): whether the returned list is a copy or a live view is not specified (ruling D29 (a), EVT-020); Java returns List.copyOf, Rust a clone, and TypeScript its own array, which a later append changes.

AC2 (old events are evicted when capacity is exceeded) is the line. Each part of it is load-bearing: the newest events, not the oldest (EVT_024_mutant_keepOldest); in append order (EVT_024_mutant_newestFirst); old events evicted at all (EVT_024_mutant_unbounded, the in-memory store); and only as many as the capacity requires (EVT_024_mutant_resetWhenFull, a store that empties itself when full). EVT-020's line (a subsequence of the appends) follows at the call (evt024_atCall).

Appends that overlap in time are kind A and outside the line, which speaks of appends made one after the other: a history is one sequence of appends in the order they take effect. Java's store is appended to from several threads (the orchestrator, action log capture, timeout handlers), and its eviction loop is not atomic, so the queue can hold a few events over capacity while appends overlap (DebugEventStore.java class comment). Rust appends under a mutex and TypeScript runs on one thread, so there no two appends overlap.

Clear: none of the three debug stores provides clear() (ruling D29 (a): clear() where provided), so a history of appends only is every history a caller can make. Closing the store changes no retained event: Java stops the broadcast, Rust and TypeScript drop the subscribers.

The capacity is kind N: it is positive and 10,000 unless the caller gives another (DEFAULT_MAX_EVENTS in all three), and a capacity that is not positive is rejected when the store is created (Java IllegalArgumentException, TypeScript Error, Rust a panic of assert!). The markdown states this without a shall, in the sentence 'A debug event store has a capacity: a positive number of events, 10,000 unless the caller gives another.', which describes the three stores as they are and is not checked by a line: the line holds at every capacity. EVT_024_default is the line at the default capacity.

The body bullet 'Session tracking' names the session identifier the store carries; it has no behaviour to state and is kind N. eventCount(), evictedCount(), size() and the replay queries eventsFrom, eventsSince and eventsBetween are not named by the spec and not modelled. The debug-aware stores answer events() from their primary store, not from the debug store, and are outside the line (EVT-020 covers them).
The body bullet 'Subscriptions', AC1, AC3 and the test derivation are the second block of this ID, EVT_024_B. The Python binding has no debug store; its live subscriptions are EVT-031.

requirements.title: DebugEventStore (subscriptions)
requirements.statement:
fun {E} S ↦
  S [] ∧
    (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
        S tr → dropped tr = false → ∀ (e : E), S (tr ++ [SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e)])) ∧
      (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
          S tr →
            ∀ (k i : ℕ),
              (received i (List.take k tr)).Sublist
                (appended (storeOps (List.take k tr)))) ∧
        (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
            S tr →
              dropped tr = false →
                ∃ j,
                  subParams j tr = none ∧
                    S (tr ++ [SubLbl.subscribe j (fun x ↦ true) none 1])) ∧
          ∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
            S tr →
              (∀ l ∈ tr, l.DebugForm) →
                dropped tr = false →
                  ∀ (i : ℕ),
                    (subParams i tr).isSome = true →
                      ∃ tr',
                        (∀ l ∈ tr', evt024Receive l = true) ∧
                          S (tr ++ tr') ∧ appendsAfter i tr <:+ received i (tr ++ tr')
requirements.scope: the debug event store's live subscriptions (Java DebugEventStore.subscribe, TypeScript DebugEventStore.subscribe, Rust libpetri-debug DebugEventStore::subscribe)
reading: For every store S with live subscriptions over any event type E, observed as the label sequences it allows:
S allows the empty run (a new store);
in every run in which the store was not dropped, an append of any event can come next;
in every run and at every point of it (every prefix), what each subscription i has received is a sublist of the events appended so far, in append order;
in every run in which the store was not dropped, a debug subscriber (every event matches, unbounded channel, one event per delivery) can subscribe next, under a number no subscription of the run has;

in every run of debug-form labels in which the store was not dropped, every subscription i made in it can go on, with receives only (no store operation, subscribe, close or drop of the store), to a run that S allows in which what i received ends with every event appended since i subscribed.
quotes: *When* an event is appended to an open debug event store, the append *shall* complete without waiting for any subscriber to receive the event.
Each subscriber of a debug event store *shall* receive only events appended to the store, each at most once and, for appends that do not overlap in time, in the order they were appended.
A subscriber may receive an event after the append that added it has returned.
*While* a debug event store is open, a caller *shall* be able to add a further subscriber, whatever subscribers the store already has.

*While* a debug event store is open, each subscriber that has not cancelled its subscription *shall* still be able to receive every event appended since it subscribed, whatever the other subscribers have received.
assumes: The model is a store with live subscriptions observed as the label sequences it allows, S : SubSem E (RefSub, Reference/Subscriptions.lean): store operations, subscribes numbered 0, 1, 2 in the order made, the start of a receive, a take from the channel, a returned batch, the end of a stream, a close and the drop of the store. A debug store subscribes in one form (SubLbl.DebugForm: every event matches, the channel is unbounded, each delivery is one event, no close label), and the witness is the reference restricted to that form, refDebugSub. Java and TypeScript subscribers are callbacks the store calls; a call delivering one event is read as a receive that returns that event (await, pull, recv). Rust's subscriber reads a crossbeam channel, which the labels describe directly.

Line 1 is the start of the observation: a new store allows the empty run. Line 2 is the first quoted sentence: an append never waits on a subscriber, so in every open run an append can come next (Java hands the broadcast to its broadcast thread, TypeScript to a microtask, and Rust sends on unbounded channels inside the store's lock). Without them a store that allows no run, or no append once someone subscribed, would meet the other lines without delivering anything (EVT_024_B_mutant_empty, EVT_024_B_mutant_noLateAppend).

Line 3 is the second quoted sentence, the order per subscriber of rulings D29 (a) and EVT-C4 (a). It compares with every event appended in the run, not only with those appended after the subscriber subscribed, because Java's broadcast task reads the subscriber list when it runs: a subscriber added between an append and its broadcast can receive that earlier event (clash evt-c#4). The reference is forward-only (refSub_received); EVT-031 states the forward-only form for its own store. The line is checked at every prefix of a run, not only on whole runs, because S is any set of label sequences and the glossary does not require it to be closed under prefixes: a store that hands out an event before it is appended is caught at the point of the delivery (EVT_024_B_mutant_early). Each clause of the sentence has its own mutant: delivered before its append, so not yet an appended event (EVT_024_B_mutant_early); delivered twice (EVT_024_B_mutant_twice); delivered newest first (EVT_024_B_mutant_lifo). The third quoted sentence is why no line ties a delivery to its append: Rust delivers inside append, TypeScript in a microtask over the subscribers present at the append, Java on a broadcast thread. Appends that overlap in time are kind A and outside the line, which a run reads in one order: in Java two threads can store e1 and e2 and broadcast e2 before e1, which the clause on overlapping appends excludes. The label model puts every append of a run in one order, so for overlapping appends a Java run is read in the order of their broadcasts; that is a modelling choice, and the only place where line 3 is stricter than the sentence it quotes.

Line 4 is the fourth quoted sentence and AC3 (multiple subscribers can be active simultaneously): a store that serves one subscriber at a time meets every other line and fails it (EVT_024_B_mutant_single).

Line 5 is the fifth quoted sentence and AC1 (while the store is open, each subscriber that has not cancelled can receive the events appended since it subscribed, each at most once and, for appends that do not overlap in time, in the order they were appended; with line 3). It is a possibility, not a guarantee: that the deliveries do happen, every event eventually reaching every subscriber that stays subscribed, is liveness and kind A, under the ideal run in which the store's broadcast runs and every subscriber returns. 'Whatever the other subscribers have received' is the quantifier over every run; the continuation may hold other subscribers' receives, since in Java and TypeScript one broadcast calls the subscribers in turn. The continuation holds receives only (evt024Receive: the start of a receive, a take, a returned batch, the end of a stream), so the store stays open while i catches up, as the sentence's While clause requires, and no subscription is added or closed on the way. A store that delivers nothing while open and flushes every subscriber in close() meets lines 1 to 4 and a line 5 whose continuation only excludes store operations, and fails line 5 (EVT_024_B_mutant_flushOnClose). Its conclusion is a suffix, not an equality, for the earlier event line 3 allows in Java. A store that delivers to its first subscriber only meets every other line and fails it (EVT_024_B_mutant_firstOnly).

Cancel is not modelled: the debug form has no close label, and line 5's debug-form premise is the 'has not cancelled' of the sentence. Java and TypeScript Subscription.cancel() remove the subscriber; Rust's Subscription::cancel only drops a sender nobody reads, so a Rust subscriber that cancelled keeps receiving (rust/libpetri-debug/src/debug_event_store.rs:36-38, :129), which no line forbids.

Open: the drop label is the store's close(), and the sentence 'A debug event store is open until its close() is called.' defines the open state the lines speak of. Lines 2, 4 and 5 speak of runs before it ('while open'), and line 5's continuation does not close the store. After close() Java still stores events but stops its broadcast (shutdownBroadcast, which waits up to two seconds for pending broadcasts), and Rust and TypeScript remove every subscriber; appends after close() are outside the reference, where no operation follows a drop, and line 3 covers whatever such a store still delivers. A subscriber that throws is caught and the broadcast goes on to the next one in Java and TypeScript; exceptions are not modelled.

The test derivation (subscribe to the debug store, append an event, verify that the subscriber receives it) is EVT_024_B_nonvacuous, with two subscribers that both receive the event appended after they subscribed, which is also the AC3 witness. The capacity of the store (AC2) is the first block of this ID, EVT_024. EVT-031 is the Python binding's subscription store over the same model, with filters, bounded channels and batches.

requirements.title: Session Archive Format
requirements.statement:
fun {D E} [SameContent D] [SameContent E] C ↦
  (∀ (a : Archive D E),
      a.WellFormed → ∃ r, C.read a = Except.ok r ∧ r.variant.toNat = a.version) ∧
    (∀ (a : Archive D E),
        a.version ∉ [1, 2, 3] → C.read a = Except.error (unsupportedMsg a.version)) ∧
      (∃ η,
          ∀ (a : Archive D E) (r : ArchiveRead D E),
            a.WellFormed →
              C.read a = Except.ok r →
                r.eventCount = a.eventCount ∧
                  r.events = List.map η a.recs ∧
                    SameContent.same r.data a.data ∧ r.metadata = a.metadata) ∧
        (∀ (S : StoreObs E) (h dh : List (StoreOp E)) (w : ArchiveVer) (d : D)
            (a : Archive D E),
            C.write S h dh w d a → a.version = w.toNat ∧ SameContent.same a.data d) ∧
          (∀ (S : StoreObs E) (h dh : List (StoreOp E)) (w : ArchiveVer) (d : D)
              (a : Archive D E),
              C.write S h dh w d a →
                ∃ l,
                  ReadDuring S h dh l ∧
                    a.eventCount = l.length ∧
                      a.metadata = archiveMeta w l ∧ SameRecs a.recs l) ∧
            (∀ (S : StoreObs E) (h : List (StoreOp E)) (w : ArchiveVer) (d : D)
                (a a' : Archive D E),
                C.write S h [] w d a → C.write S h [] w d a' → a = a') ∧
              ∀ (S : StoreObs E) (h dh : List (StoreOp E)) (w : ArchiveVer) (d : D),
                ∃ a, C.write S h dh w d a
requirements.scope: where an implementation provides session archives: the Java, TypeScript and Rust SessionArchiveWriter and SessionArchiveReader, and Python's, which run Rust's
reading: For every archive codec C (an implementation's writer and reader) over session header fields D and events E, each with its notion of same content (the same JSON value, read as an unordered object):

for every well-formed archive a (its version is that of a variant w, and its eventCount, its metadata and its body come from one list of events l as the writer forms them), the reader returns a result whose variant is the variant of a's version;
for every archive a whose header version v is not 1, 2 or 3, the reader fails with the message Unsupported archive version: v (reader supports 1..3);

there is one hydration function η such that, whenever the reader returns r for a well-formed archive a, r carries the eventCount of a, the events η applied to each record of a in body order, header fields of the same content as those of a, and the metadata of a;
every archive the writer writes for version w and session fields d carries the number of w as its version and header fields of the same content as d;

for every archive a the writer writes for version w from a store S with history h while the operations dh run, some list l that a call of events() on S returns during the write is the source of all of a: the eventCount of a is the length of l, the metadata of a is that of l for w (none for V1), and the body of a is, record by record, of the same content as l;
two archives the writer writes for the same version and session fields, from the same store and history with no operation during the write, are equal;
for every store, history, operations during the write, version and session fields, the writer writes some archive.
quotes: *Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its reader reads a well-formed archive of header version 1, 2 or 3 in its own implementation's format (one whose `eventCount` and metadata are those of its body, as its writer writes them), the reader *shall* return the header variant of that version (`V1`, `V2` or `V3`).

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *if* its reader reads an archive in its own implementation's format whose header version is not 1, 2 or 3, *then* the reader *shall* reject the archive with the error `Unsupported archive version: <version> (reader supports 1..3)`, which names the version it found and the supported range.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its reader accepts a well-formed archive in its own implementation's format, it *shall* return the header's `eventCount` unchanged, the header's session fields and metadata as written, and one event for each record of the body, in body order.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its writer writes an archive of a session for header version 1, 2 or 3 (`writeV1`, `writeV2`, or `write` for version 3), the header *shall* carry that version and the session's own header fields.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, *when* its writer writes an archive, the writer *shall* take one snapshot of the event store, the header's `eventCount` *shall* be the number of events in that snapshot, a V1 header *shall* carry no metadata, the V2 and V3 metadata *shall* be computed from that snapshot, and the body *shall* hold one record for each event of that snapshot, in the order of the snapshot.
