*Where* an implementation provides session archives, two archives its writer writes for the same header version from identical run data *shall* be identical.

*Where* an implementation provides session archives, its writer *shall* write an archive of any session for each of the header versions 1, 2 and 3 (`writeV1`, `writeV2`, and `write` for version 3), whatever the session's event store holds.
assumes: The model is an archive codec C : ArchiveCodec D E (glossary in Reference/Archive.lean: Archive codec, Session archive, Same content, Well-formed archive). Its writer is a relation, write S h dh w d a: writing header version w for a session with header fields d, whose event store S has the history h when the write starts and runs the operations dh during the write, can produce the archive a. Its reader is a function, read a. An archive is the header version tag as written (a number, since a reader can meet any number), the session's own header fields (opaque: session id, net name, DOT diagram, start and end time, tags, net structure), eventCount, the V2/V3 metadata and the body. A record is the event it records, as rendered. The store is the glossary's StoreObs, so the lines hold for any store a session has: an in-memory store, the bounded debug store of a debug session (EVT-024), or another.

Same content (SameContent) is how the key order sentences ('Key order in an archive is not guaranteed, and [CORE-073]'s canonical order does not reach it.', and a JSON object as an unordered collection) reach the model: two values are the same content when they render the same JSON value read as an unordered object, so a list of key and value entries (a marking in the snapshot form, a tag map) is the same content as any permutation of it, and a value with no object inside is the same content only as itself. Lines 3, 4 and 5 compare header fields and records up to same content, and line 6 compares two archives exactly. So a writer that renders every marking in one fixed key order meets EVT-025 (EVT_025_allows_fixedOrder: JavaScript's numeric-first key order is 'arbitrary but fixed, so it satisfies this'), and a writer that renders it in a per-process order does not (EVT_025_forbids_seededMarking, line 6). Same content is part of the model of the header and event types; the evidence uses equality for numbers and the unit type, and permutation for lists of entries. 'A host needing a byte-stable archive artefact across implementations MUST canonicalise at its own serialization boundary' binds the host, not the implementation: it is an assumption about callers (kind A), not a line.

Not modelled, kind N: the bytes (the length prefixes, the JSON text, LZ4 compression in Java and gzip in TypeScript, Rust and Python), I/O and serialization errors, which fields of the header table V1 has and V2 adds beyond the metadata, the encoding of time values, the per-language token shapes of the body, and the security note. The body sentence on the archive's shape, a versioned header followed by one length-prefixed JSON record per event, is lines 4 and 5 without the framing. The metadata is a stand-in (ArchiveMeta: the number of events and the first and last event) for the runtimes' event-type histogram, first and last timestamp and hasErrors flag, which read the event kind and timestamp. Line 5 fixes it to the stand-in of the snapshot (archiveMeta, none for a V1 header), so a writer whose header metadata does not describe its snapshot violates it (EVT_025_forbids_emptyMeta: the reader's empty fallback written into every V2/V3 header), while what the histogram holds beyond the stand-in is configuration.

The body sentence that readers MUST accept all three versions and dispatch into the matching sealed variant (V1/V2/V3) is line 1 and the first quoted sentence. Lines 1 and 3 bind the well-formed archives (Archive.WellFormed: the version is 1, 2 or 3, and the count, the metadata and the body come from one list of events, which lines 4 and 5 make true of every archive a writer writes, evt025_written_wf), so a reader may reject an archive whose eventCount disagrees with its body (EVT_025_allows_strictReader); line 2 binds every archive. AC2 is lines 1 and 2 and the first two quoted sentences. The error text of line 2 is the message all three readers produce (rust/libpetri-debug/src/archive/session_archive_reader.rs parse_header, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/debug/archive/SessionArchiveReader.java readHeader, typescript/src/debug/archive/session-archive-reader.ts parseHeader); it fixes the exact text where AC2 asks only that the error name the version and the supported range, an added requirement that no runtime fails. Python raises it as a ValueError from Rust's reader. Errors of a truncated or corrupt byte stream are outside the model, which has no bytes.

Line 3 is the third quoted sentence: the reader returns the header as written (eventCount unchanged, the session fields up to same content, the metadata), so a reader that loses the metadata of a V2/V3 header violates it (EVT_025_forbids_dropsMetadata: a Java header record component renamed away from its wire name and read as null, since the header mapper ignores unknown properties), and the events are the records, each hydrated by one function η of the reader, in body order (EVT_025_forbids_reversedEvents). Hydration is lossy by design (a Java Token<JsonNode>, a Rust ReplayedTokenPayload), so line 3 fixes the number and order of the events, not their content. 'the header's session fields and metadata as written' and 'in body order' are new text: the markdown said that the reader dispatches into the variant and, in AC8, that the count matches the events (map evt-c, EVT-025). Every reader meets them: each returns the header it parsed and reads the records in sequence.

AC1 is lines 4 and 7. Line 7, the seventh quoted sentence, says that the writer writes every header version for every session and store: writeV1 and writeV2 exist (EVT_025_forbids_v3Only), and a writer that refuses a store that has evicted, instead of counting what it retained, violates it (EVT_025_mutant_refuses: the 1.8.2 lifetime-counter bug of rust/libpetri-debug/src/archive/session_archive_writer.rs write_v1 'fixed' with a guard). Line 4 says that writeV1 and writeV2 write the header of their version and write (writeV3) version 3 (EVT_025_mutant_currentHeader), and that the header carries the session's own fields (EVT_025_mutant_wrongSession). That the default writer is the version 3 one is the naming of the API, and that the event body has the writer's current token shape whatever the header version is the token shape; both are kind N, since a record is the event, not its token shape.

AC8 is lines 3 and 5. Line 5 is the AC's 'the writer MUST take exactly one snapshot of the event store; header eventCount, V2/V3 metadata, and the event body MUST all derive from that single snapshot': one list l that a call of events() returns during the write gives the count (its length), the metadata (archiveMeta of the version and l) and the body (l, record by record up to same content). The operations dh during the write stand for another thread still appending (the debug stores take appends from the executor while a writer runs); without them one read and two reads could not be told apart. A writer that takes the header from one read and the body from a later one violates line 5 even when the two reads have the same length (EVT_025_mutant_twoReads, on the bounded store). 'Implementations MUST NOT populate eventCount from a cumulative lifetime counter' is line 5 too: on the bounded debug store the count of every append ever made overstates the retained events (EVT_025_mutant_lifetime; the write_v1 bug of libpetri 1.8.2 and earlier). The round trip archive.eventCount() == archive.events().size() for all three header versions is the consequence evt025_roundtrip of lines 1, 3, 4 and 5, and evt025_bounded shows that an archive of the bounded store never counts more than its capacity.

Line 5's 'in the order of the snapshot' and 'a V1 header shall carry no metadata' are new text: the body's 'one length-prefixed JSON record per event' fixed the number of records and not their order, and the header table says that V1 has no metadata only by listing what v2 adds (map evt-c, EVT-025). Every writer meets them, since each walks the one list it took (write_framed in Rust, writeFramed in Java and TypeScript) and writes its V1 header without metadata.

AC3, AC4, AC5, AC6 and AC7 are kind N: they fix the per-language token shapes and how a reader hydrates them (AC3 Java's typed round trip, AC4 its Token<JsonNode> fallback, AC5 the structured payload TypeScript and Rust preserve, AC6 legacy {value, valueType} tokens read as strings, AC7 TypeScript omitting an empty structured field). Line 3 keeps of them that hydration gives one event per record, in body order, whatever the token shape (AC4: the Java deserializer never throws on an unknown type). The model cannot tell a typed token from a JSON node; a reader that skips the records it cannot hydrate violates line 3 (EVT_025_mutant_skips).

The reproducibility paragraph is line 6. 'An archive written twice by the same implementation from identical run data MUST NOT differ' is line 6: identical run data are the same store, history and session fields with no operation during the write, and the writer is a relation so that a writer whose output depends on something outside the run data, such as a per-process hash seed, is a codec too. That an implementation MUST NOT put a per-process-randomised map on the path to the archive is line 6 for the archive: a writer that renders a marking inside an event in a per-process order (EVT_025_forbids_seededMarking) or a map of the header in a per-process order (EVT_025_mutant_seededTags) writes two archives from one run's data. Rendering in one fixed order is not that (EVT_025_allows_fixedOrder). The debug protocol half of that sentence is not stated here.

The header table's 'identical across languages', 'only headers are' byte-compatible, and TypeScript and Rust bodies being wire-compatible are reworded under ruling D29 (a) (clashes evt-c#5 and evt-c#6): headers, and TypeScript and Rust bodies, share field names and JSON types but not the encoding of time values (ISO-8601 text in Java and TypeScript, decimal epoch milliseconds in Rust and Python), so an archive is read correctly only by the language that wrote it. No line compares archives across languages, and lines 1 to 3 bind a reader on archives in its own implementation's format only: the codec C is one implementation's, and an archive of another language's compression or time encoding is outside the lines (Java's reader cannot decompress a gzip archive, Rust's reader rejects ISO-8601 event timestamps, and TypeScript's reads decimal epoch milliseconds as invalid dates).

Priority is SHOULD while the body says MUST, so every quoted sentence reads 'Where an implementation provides session archives' (ruling D20, EVT-C11 (a) item 5). Java, TypeScript, Rust and Python provide them.

Two runtimes fail a line at HEAD. The user kept the lines and recorded the gaps as runtime defects (spec/runtime-defects.md, and the Known gap sentences of the markdown's implementation notes). Java's V2/V3 header renders the metadata histogram and the tags through Map.copyOf, whose iteration order is randomised per JVM, and Jackson writes a map in iteration order, so one session archived by two JVMs gives two different headers (line 6, RD-17; the model shows it on the tags, EVT_025_mutant_seededTags; java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/debug/archive/SessionMetadata.java canonical constructor, SessionArchive.java V2 and V3, SessionArchiveWriter.java writeV2 and writeV3). Python's write_from_store copies the store's events into a debug store of the default capacity 10,000 before writing, so a store of more events is archived without its oldest ones (line 5, RD-18; rust/libpetri-py/src/archive.rs; EVT_025_forbids_copyThroughBounded, with capacity 1). Python's writer offers version 3 only: write_from_store calls Rust's SessionArchiveWriter::write, and Python has no writeV1 or writeV2, which AC1 asks of each language (line 7, RD-19; EVT_025_forbids_v3Only). For a store with no events write_from_store takes the session's start and end times from the wall clock (SystemTime::now), so two archives of the same empty session differ (line 6, RD-20; rust/libpetri-py/src/archive.rs).

The test derivation (round trips, unknown-version rejection, explicit v2 emission) is EVT_025_nonvacuous on the reference: a version 3 archive of a bounded store after an eviction counts its two retained events, not the three appends, and reads back as V3 with that count, its metadata and two events; a version 2 archive carries version 2 and its metadata; an archive of version 99 is rejected with the message naming 99.

requirements.title: Event Filtering
requirements.statement:
fun {E} sh H ↦
  (∀ (q : EventQuery) (es : List E),
      q.namesNoEmpty = true →
        H.select q.unpaged es = List.filter (fun e ↦ q.matches (sh e)) es) ∧
    (∀ (q : EventQuery) (es : List E), H.select q es = q.page (H.select q.unpaged es)) ∧
      (∀ (es : List E), H.failures es = List.filter (fun e ↦ (sh e).type.isFailure) es) ∧
        (∀ (es : List E), (List.map Prod.fst (H.counters es)).Nodup) ∧
          (∀ (es : List E) (k : EventType) (n : ℕ),
              (k, n) ∈ H.counters es ↔ n = countOfType sh k es ∧ n ≠ 0) ∧
            ∀ (ts : Option (List EventType)) (es : List E),
              H.count ts es =
                (List.filter (fun e ↦ Option.all (fun l ↦ l.contains (sh e).type) ts)
                    es).length
requirements.scope: the event query helpers where an implementation provides them (type, transition and failure helpers and the event count in Java and TypeScript; transition and failure helpers and the event count in Rust; every helper in the Python binding)
reading: For every event type E, every shape function sh and the helpers H, over every list es of events (the list events() returns):

a query q without paging whose transition filter does not name the empty name returns the events of es that match every filter of q (type among its types, a transition name among its names, a place name among its names), in the order of es;
a query q returns the page of its unpaged answer: it skips the first offset events and keeps the first limit of the rest;
failures() returns the events of es whose type is TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut or ActionTimedOut, in the order of es;
counters() names no event type twice;
counters() holds the pair (k, n) exactly when n is the number of events of es of type k and n is not zero;
the count for the types ts is the number of events of es whose type is in ts, and the number of events of es when no type is given.
quotes: *Where* an implementation provides a query over the events of an event store, the query without offset and limit *shall* return exactly the events that `events()` returns and that match every filter the query gives, in the order `events()` returns them, for every query whose transition filter does not name the empty name.

A filter by event type *shall* match the events of the given types, a filter by transition name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given transition names, and a filter by place name *shall* match the events that carry one of the given place names.
An event that carries no transition name *shall* match no filter by transition name, and its presence in the store *shall not* change which other events such a filter returns.

*Where* an implementation provides offset and limit on a query, the query *shall* skip the first `offset` matching events and return the first `limit` of the matching events that follow (all of them when no limit is given), so that the page is taken over the filtered result and not over the store.

*Where* an implementation provides `failures()`, it *shall* return exactly the TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut and ActionTimedOut events that `events()` returns, in the order `events()` returns them.

*Where* an implementation provides `counters()`, it *shall* name each event type that occurs among the events `events()` returns exactly once, with the number of those events of that type, and *shall* name no other event type.

*Where* an implementation provides a count of events, the count *shall* be the number of events that `events()` returns whose type is one of the given types, or the number of all of them when no type is given.
assumes: The model is the helpers of one implementation, H : QueryHelpers E, each applied to the list es that a call of events() returns, and the shape of an event, sh : E → EventShape: its type (one of the thirteen of EVT-002 to EVT-014), the transition name it carries and the place name it carries. The helpers read nothing else of an event, so the event type E and its shape are parameters; which kinds carry a name is the event model's (wave W7): the eight transition kinds, LogMessage included, carry a transition name, and only TokenAdded and TokenRemoved carry a place name (net_event.rs transition_name and place_name; net-event.ts eventTransitionName). Events with equal shapes are told apart by position in es, so the lines fix which events a helper returns, not only their shapes.

Scope (ruling D20, clash evt-c#16, EVT-C11): the helpers differ per language, and each line constrains a helper only where an implementation provides it. Lines 1 and 2 read only select, line 3 only failures, lines 4 and 5 only counters and line 6 only count, so the lines of a helper an implementation lacks constrain nothing it has. Java and TypeScript provide eventsOfType (a query with one type), transitionEvents (one transition name), failures() and size() (the count with no type); Rust's in-memory store provides transition_events, failures(), size() and a predicate filter, but no type filter; the Python binding provides the full query (sets of types, transitions and places, offset and limit), len(), count(types=...), counters() and failures() (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs). The spec edit of this wave adds an implementation-status line that says so.

The first three quoted sentences are line 1. Filters given together combine by 'and' (the Python binding's FilterSpec.matches), so a query with both a transition filter and a place filter returns nothing in the current event model; the spec says nothing else, and the line follows the one implementation that offers both. The order is the order of es, which on an in-memory store is append order (evt030_mem_select, through EVT-021).

The empty name: every runtime fills the transition name of an engine diagnostic at the initial-marking seam with the empty name (Java BitmapNetExecutor warnUnknownPlace(..., ""), bitmap-net-executor.ts warnUnknownPlace(place, ''), Rust emit_unknown_place_warnings(&dead, "")), and EVT-013 reads such an event as one that carries no transition name. A filter for the empty name would then ask for the engine diagnostics, which the spec leaves open; line 1 constrains every query whose transition filter does not name the empty name, as the first quoted sentence and the implementation-status line say. Under that guard the reading of the empty name does not matter: helpers that compare names as they are meet EVT-030 under the shape that reads the empty name as no name (EVT_030_allows_emptySentinel), so the third quoted sentence applies to Rust and Python with the shape EVT-013 describes. A transition named by the empty name is not ruled out by any requirement; its events are told apart from engine diagnostics by no runtime, and a filter for it is outside the line.

The third quoted sentence and ruling D29 (a) (EVT-C10 (a)): every helper is a total function, and an event with no transition name matches no transition filter. Java's transitionEvents calls equals on the transition name of every LogMessage and throws on an engine diagnostic whose name is null, which both Java executors emit on an interrupted run (clash evt-c#13); EVT_030_mutant_throwsOnNameless models that call as one that returns nothing, and line 1 rejects it. It is a recorded gap in Java (RD-21 in spec/runtime-defects.md), to be fixed outside this migration; the implementation-status line names it. TypeScript compares an optional name and Rust an Option, and both return the matching events.

The fourth quoted sentence is line 2: the page is taken of the filtered answer, which the Python binding does (filter, then skip offset, then take limit). A helper that pages the store and then filters breaks it (EVT_030_mutant_pageFirst).

The fifth quoted sentence is line 3 (AC4). The failure set is the one EVT-023 logs at the failure level (ruling D29 (a), the level table failures first); all four runtimes test the same three kinds (EventStore.java failures, net-event.ts isFailureEvent, net_event.rs is_failure).

The sixth quoted sentence is lines 4 and 5 (AC5). The histogram is a list of pairs whose order is not fixed: Python returns a dict in ascending order of the type name, and the order of a dict is not part of the requirement. A type with no events has no entry, as in Python, whose counters() builds an entry only for a type it meets. evt030_counters_sum derives AC5's 'values sum to the total event count' from lines 4 and 5 for every helper that meets them.

The seventh quoted sentence is line 6, the body's 'Count events': the count with no type is size() in Java, TypeScript and Rust and len() or count() in Python; count(types=...) in Python is the count by type, which Python computes on its own path rather than as the length of a query. An empty type set counts no event (EVT_030_mutant_emptyTypesCountsAll). evt030_count_all and evt030_count_select tie the count to the number of events and to the length of the type query.

AC1 (eventsOfType(TransitionCompleted) returns only completed events) is line 1 at a query with one type (evt030_eventsOfType); AC2 (transitionEvents returns the events of that transition) is line 1 at a query with one transition name, read as the events that carry that name (ruling D29 (a); the spec edit of this wave rewords AC2 to say so): TokenAdded and TokenRemoved events of the transition's firing carry no transition name and are not returned in any runtime (evt030_transitionEvents); AC3 (place filter, offset and limit) is lines 1 and 2, and its 'only token events' follows once the event model gives only TokenAdded and TokenRemoved a place name (evt030_placeEvents takes that as a premise; wave W7 discharges it when GlossaryEvents lands).
The test derivation (a run with mixed events; each filter, the paging, the histogram and the count give the right subsets and totals) is EVT_030_nonvacuous on a decided list of mixed events.

requirements.title: EventStore Live Subscriptions
requirements.statement:
fun {E} S ↦
  (∀ (tr tr' : List (SubLbl E)),
      S (tr ++ tr') → ∀ (i : ℕ), (received i tr).Sublist (matchingAfter i tr)) ∧
    (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
        S tr →
          ∀ (i : ℕ),
            ∀ b ∈ batches i tr,
              b ≠ [] ∧ ∃ f c n, subParams i tr = some (f, c, n) ∧ b.length ≤ n) ∧
      (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
          S tr →
            ∀ (i : ℕ) (f : E → Bool) (c : Option ℕ) (n : ℕ),
              subParams i tr = some (f, c, n) → c.isSome = true) ∧
        (∀ (pre : List (SubLbl E)) (e : E) (suf : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ) (f : E → Bool)
            (c n : ℕ),
            S (pre ++ SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e) :: suf) →
              subParams i pre = some (f, some c, n) →
                f e = true →
                  c ≤ backlog i pre →
                    (received i (pre ++ SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e) :: suf)).Sublist
                      (matchingAfter i pre)) ∧
          (∀ (pre : List (SubLbl E)) (e : E) (mid : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ)
              (f : E → Bool) (c n : ℕ),
              S (pre ++ SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e) :: mid) →
                subParams i pre = some (f, some c, n) →
                  f e = true →
                    c ≤ backlog i pre →
                      pending i pre = false →
                        evt031Quiet i mid = true →
                          ∃ bs,
                            S
                              (pre ++
                                SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e) ::
                                  (mid ++ evt031Recvs i bs ++
                                    [SubLbl.await i, SubLbl.finish i]))) ∧
            (∀ (pre : List (SubLbl E)) (e : E) (mid : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ)
                (f : E → Bool) (c n : ℕ),
                S (pre ++ SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e) :: (mid ++ [SubLbl.finish i])) →
                  subParams i pre = some (f, some c, n) →
                    f e = true →
                      c ≤ backlog i pre →
                        evt031Ended i pre = false →
                          pending i pre = false →
                            evt031NoClose i mid = true →
                              received i mid = evt031Held i pre) ∧
              (∀ (tr : List (SubLbl E)),
                  S tr →
                    dropped tr = false →
                      ∀ (e : E), S (tr ++ [SubLbl.op (StoreOp.append e)])) ∧
                (∀ (pre suf : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ),
                    S (pre ++ SubLbl.close i :: suf) →
                      (subParams i pre).isSome = true →
                        pending i pre = false → received i suf = []) ∧
                  (∀ (pre mid : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ),
                      S (pre ++ SubLbl.close i :: mid) →
                        (subParams i pre).isSome = true →
                          pending i pre = false →
                            evt031Quiet i mid = true →
                              S
                                (pre ++
                                  SubLbl.close i ::
                                    (mid ++ [SubLbl.await i, SubLbl.finish i]))) ∧
                    (∀ (pre mid : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ),
                        S (pre ++ SubLbl.drop :: mid) →
                          (subParams i pre).isSome = true →
                            pending i pre = false →
                              evt031Quiet i mid = true →
                                ∃ bs,
                                  S
                                    (pre ++
                                      SubLbl.drop ::
                                        (mid ++ evt031Recvs i bs ++
                                          [SubLbl.await i, SubLbl.finish i]))) ∧
                      ∀ (pre mid : List (SubLbl E)) (i : ℕ),
                        S (pre ++ SubLbl.drop :: (mid ++ [SubLbl.finish i])) →
                          (subParams i pre).isSome = true →
                            evt031Ended i pre = false →
                              pending i pre = false →
                                evt031NoClose i mid = true →
                                  received i mid = evt031Held i pre
requirements.scope: the live subscriptions of an event store, where an implementation provides them: the Python binding's InMemoryEventStore (subscribe and subscribe_stream, run on Rust in rust/libpetri-py); Java and TypeScript pending, and the Rust crate's own InMemoryEventStore has none
reading: For every store with live subscriptions S over any event type E (S is the set of label sequences the store allows):

1. at every point of every run of S, what each subscription i has received so far, its batches concatenated, is a sublist of the events appended after i subscribed and before that point that its filter matches;
2. every batch i received in a run of S is non-empty, and i subscribed with a batch size of at least its length;
3. every subscription made in a run of S has a finite channel capacity;

4. if an append of an event that the filter of i matches finds the channel of i full (i subscribed with capacity c, and its backlog, the matching events appended since it subscribed that no receive took, has reached c), then over the whole run i received only matching events appended before that append;

5. after such an append made while no receive of i was pending, followed by any labels none of which is i's own, S allows receives of i that return some batches, followed by a receive that reports the end;

6. if moreover i had not ended before that append (by an earlier such append, a close made while no receive of i was pending, or the drop), then whenever a receive of i reports the end after it with no close of i in between, the events i received in between are exactly the events its channel held: the matching events appended since it subscribed, less as many as its receives took;
7. after every run of S in which the store was not dropped, S allows one more append;
8. after a close of a subscription i made before, while no receive of i was pending, i receives nothing;
9. after such a close, followed by any labels none of which is i's own, S allows a receive of i that reports the end;

10. after the drop of the store, for every subscription i made before with no receive pending, followed by any labels none of which is i's own, S allows receives of i that return some batches, followed by a receive that reports the end;

11. if moreover i had not ended before the drop, then whenever a receive of i reports the end after the drop with no close of i in between, the events i received in between are exactly the events its channel held at the drop.
quotes: *Where* an event store provides live subscriptions, the events a subscription has received at any point, taken over all its batches in the order it received them, *shall* be events that match its filters and were appended to the store after the subscription was created and before that point, in append order, each at most once.
Each batch a subscription receives *shall* hold at least one event and at most `batch_size` events, so that with `batch_size = 1` it receives one event per batch.
Each subscription *shall* have a finite channel capacity.

*When* an append of an event that matches the filters of a subscription finds its channel full, the store *shall* end that subscription: the subscription *shall* receive no event appended from then on, and, if none of its receives is pending at that append, its receives *shall* take the events its channel holds and then report the end of the stream, unless the subscription is closed first.
Until the store is dropped, an append *shall* be accepted at every point; in particular it *shall not* wait for room in the channel of a subscription.
*When* a subscription is closed while none of its receives is pending, it *shall* receive no further event, and its next receive *shall* report the end of the stream.

*When* the store is dropped, the receives of each of its subscriptions that has no receive pending *shall* take the events its channel holds and then report the end of the stream, unless the subscription is closed first.
assumes: The model is the observation of one store with live subscriptions, S : SubSem E (Reference/Subscriptions.lean): the label sequences it allows. A label is a store operation (op), a subscribe with a filter, a channel capacity (none: unbounded) and a batch size, the start of a receive (await), a take of the oldest event from the channel by the pending receive (pull), a returned batch (recv), a reported end of the stream (finish, Python's StopAsyncIteration), a close, or the drop of the store. The observation functions received, batches, subParams, matchingAfter, backlog and pending, and the block-local evt031Own and evt031Quiet (the labels of a subscription), evt031NoClose, evt031Recvs (receives returning given batches), evt031Held (the events the channel holds, by the labels) and evt031Ended (an overflow, a close with no receive pending, or the drop happened), read the labels only. The event type E is a parameter: the lines say nothing about what an event holds.

Filters: a filter is a predicate on events. Which events a filter by type, transition and place matches is the matching rule of [EVT-030]; the Python binding evaluates both with one FilterSpec (rust/libpetri-py/src/events.rs), and this block does not restate the rule. AC1 and the first quoted sentence are line 1: a sublist of the matching events appended after the subscribe is filtered, in append order and at most once, and AC2 (forward-only) is its 'after'. Line 1 is stated at every point of a run, not on whole runs only, so a receive cannot return an event before that event is appended (mutant EVT_031_mutant_early); S need not be closed under prefixes.

Batches: AC3 and the second quoted sentence are line 2; a store whose receive may return an empty batch meets every other line and the batch-size half of line 2, and fails it (EVT_031_mutant_emptyBatch); evt031_unary derives one event per batch from a batch size of 1, whatever the timeout, which is the runtime's behaviour (the batch loop runs only when batch_size > 1). The batch timeout, 'flushing early after batch_timeout_ms' in AC3 and the markdown sentence '*When* a receive has taken the first event of its batch, it *shall* add further events until the batch holds `batch_size` events, `batch_timeout_ms` have elapsed since it took that first event, or no further event can arrive, and *shall* then return the batch; with `batch_timeout_ms = 0` it *shall* add only the events already in the channel.', is kind T on tokio's clock, which has no seam ([TIME-015] lists no Python seam, by design): it cannot be tested on virtual time and is not modelled. Its untimed clause, a timeout of 0 adding only the events already in the channel, is not stated either, because the subscribe label carries no timeout. The model lets a receive return a non-empty batch at any moment, which every timeout meets, and lines 5 and 10 allow any batching of what the channel holds, so a receive that takes every buffered event up to batch_size, as the runtime's does, meets them (EVT_031_allows_greedy).

Capacity: the third quoted sentence is line 3. The witness evt031PySub is the reference with a finite capacity on every subscribe, the form of the Python store, whose channel_capacity is a positive integer. The reference alone also allows an unbounded channel (none), the debug stores' form of [EVT-024], and it violates line 3 (EVT_031_mutant_unboundedChannel).

Overflow (AC4 and ruling D86 (a)): the fourth quoted sentence is lines 4, 5 and 6. Line 4 names the full channel by observations: the backlog of i (matching events appended since it subscribed, less those its receives took) has reached its capacity, and the appended event matches the filter of i. Line 5 says the stream can end, at any later point, rather than hang; line 6 says it does not end before the receives have taken what the channel held, which evt031Held reads from the labels while the subscription has not ended. A close of i after the overflow ends the stream at once (lines 8 and 9), which is the clause 'unless the subscription is closed first' and why line 6 has no close of i in between. evt031_overflow_drains derives from lines 5 and 6 that the drain S allows returns exactly what the channel held. A receive pending at the overflowing append is outside the lines, as the qualifier of the sentence says. Python's capacity is always finite; line 4 speaks only of a finite one.

Append: the fifth quoted sentence is line 7: S allows an append after every run before the drop, whatever the reason a store might refuse one, and in particular an append does not wait for room in a full channel (ruling D86 (a)). In this label model a refused append and a waiting one look the same, and the Python store refuses an append only after a drop.

Close (AC4 and ruling D86 (d)): the sixth quoted sentence is lines 8 and 9, for a subscription that exists. A close made while a receive of the subscription is pending does nothing in Python (close() takes the receiver only when its lock is free; clash evt-c#8), so the pending receive keeps waiting; the lines require no receive pending, and the case is recorded in the markdown as outside the requirement. Line 9 lets other labels, such as appends, come between the close and the receive. The end of the stream is reported the same way after a close, a drop and an overflow; telling them apart would be a runtime change, so no line does.

Drop: the seventh quoted sentence is lines 10 and 11. For a subscription that ended before the drop, lines 5 and 6 (an overflow) or line 9 (a close) already say when its stream ends. After a drop the store takes no further append or subscribe, which the reference meets (refSub_dropped_no_op) and no line restates. The Python store provides no clear(); the model allows one and it changes no subscription.

Liveness is out of scope: no line says that a matching event is eventually received, only what a receive may hand over, that an end can be reached, and what is handed over before it. A store that allows no run at all meets every line; EVT_031_nonvacuous shows the premises of the lines are met by the witness. Configuration is kind N and not a line: Python's defaults (batch_size 64, batch_timeout_ms 10, channel_capacity 4096) and its rejection of a batch_size or channel_capacity of 0 with ValueError, which the model reflects by allowing no such subscribe. subscribe_stream is subscribe with batch size 1 and no list wrapper, so the same lines cover it. Subscriptions are numbered in the order they are made.

Status: the requirement is Proposed (Java and TypeScript pending). Ruling D47 (c) gives it a block now that D86 fixes the policy; the block binds every implementation that provides live subscriptions. The test derivation is EVT_031_nonvacuous: an event appended before the subscribe and a non-matching one are not delivered, the two matching ones come in one batch of size 2, and a close is followed by the end.

requirements.title: Marking Replay Cache
requirements.statement:
fun {N E} [DecidableEq N] view call ↦
  ∀ (c : Cache N) (es : List E) (i : ℕ),
    Cache.Coherent view c es →
      (call c es i).2 = Spec.replay view (List.take i es) ∧
        Cache.Coherent view (call c es i).1 es
requirements.scope: the replay cache of the debug protocol (Rust libpetri-debug MarkingCache, Python MarkingCache, Java org.libpetri.debug.MarkingCache, TypeScript MarkingCache in libpetri/debug)
reading: For every replay view view : E → REv N of an event type E onto the places N, and every call of compute_at, call : CacheCall N E:

for every cache c coherent with the stream es (every snapshot k of c stands for the index (k + 1) * iv, which is no greater than the length of es, and is the replay of the first (k + 1) * iv events of es) and every index i, the state the call answers is the replay of the first i events of es from the empty state (of all of es when i is past its length);
and the cache the call leaves is coherent with es.
quotes: *While* every snapshot in the replay cache is at an index no greater than the length of `events` and is the replay of `events` up to that index, `compute_at(events, index)` *shall* return the replay of the first `index` events of `events`, or of all of `events` when `index` is beyond its length.

*When* `compute_at(events, index)` returns, every snapshot it leaves in the replay cache *shall* be at an index no greater than the length of `events` and be the replay of `events` up to that index, provided every snapshot in the cache met both conditions before the call.

The replay of an event stream *shall* start from the empty state (no token in any place, no enabled and no in-flight transition) and apply its events in order, each as follows: a `MarkingSnapshot` sets the token count of every place it carries to the count it carries and of every other place to zero; a `TokenAdded` adds one token to its place; a `TokenRemoved` removes one token from its place, and does nothing if the place has none; a `TransitionEnabled` adds its transition to the enabled transitions; a `TransitionStarted` removes its transition from the enabled transitions and adds it to the in-flight transitions; a `TransitionCompleted`, `TransitionFailed`, `TransitionTimedOut` or `ActionTimedOut` removes its transition from the in-flight transitions; any other event (`ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionCompleted`, `TransitionClockRestarted`, `LogMessage`) leaves the state unchanged.
assumes: The model is one call of compute_at(events, index), observed as call : CacheCall N E: from the cache's content before the call (Cache N: the snapshot interval and the snapshots), the event stream and the index, the cache's content after the call and the replayed state it answers (RState N). The event type E is a parameter and view : E → REv N its replay view (glossary: Replay view), which keeps of each event only what the replay reads: the count per place of a MarkingSnapshot, the place of a TokenAdded or TokenRemoved, and the transition of a TransitionEnabled, a TransitionStarted and the four end events (TransitionCompleted, TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut, ActionTimedOut); ExecutionStarted, ExecutionCompleted, TransitionClockRestarted and LogMessage are other. The block holds for every view, and the replay rules are fixed over the view by applyEv.

Which named event takes which rule (the event names of the third quoted sentence) is recView over RecEvent N, the thirteen recorded events by name with the part the replay can read, a MarkingSnapshot carried as the list of places it lists. recView gives an unlisted place the count zero, the four end events ended, and the four other events other. The forbids evidence fixes the names at that view: a cache built over a view that treats TransitionCompleted, TransitionFailed, TransitionTimedOut or ActionTimedOut as other, or that reads TransitionClockRestarted as TransitionEnabled, violates EVT-032 at recView (one theorem per name), and so does a cache whose MarkingSnapshot keeps the old count of a place it does not list (Rust apply_events without marking.clear(); EVT_032_mutant_snapMerge). The executor event model of wave W7 defines the full event type (timestamps, token values, outputs, errors); its replay view must be recView after the map that forgets what the replay does not read, and the W7 integrator ties the two.

The third quoted sentence is the glossary's replay step applyEv, which the two lines use through replay (the from-scratch replay) and Cache.Coherent: a definition the lines are stated with, not a line of its own. A cache that replays by any other step violates line 1, one mutant per clause: a replay that ignores MarkingSnapshot, that adds a snapshot's counts to the old ones instead of replacing them, that ignores TokenAdded, that ignores TokenRemoved, that ignores TransitionEnabled, whose TransitionStarted leaves its transition enabled, whose TransitionStarted does not put its transition in flight, whose end events leave their transition in flight, or whose other events clear the enabled set. A TransitionStarted puts its transition in flight whether or not it was enabled. The rules are those of all four bindings: Rust apply_events (rust/libpetri-debug/src/marking_cache.rs), Java DebugProtocolHandler.applyEvents, TypeScript applyEvents (typescript/src/debug/debug-protocol-handler.ts), and Python, which wraps the Rust cache (rust/libpetri-py/src/marking_cache.rs).

The length bound of coherence (a snapshot stands for an index no greater than the length of the stream) is load-bearing: a cache that stores a snapshot past the end of the stream (TypeScript ensureCachedUpTo without its guard nextSnapshotIndex > events.length, where slice clamps) answers the call right and violates line 2 (EVT_032_mutant_premature); once the stream grows, the premature snapshot is read as the state at its index (evt032_premature_harm). coherentWith_append, and through it AC3, uses the bound.

The replayed state is compared by value: the token count of every place, and the enabled and the in-flight transition names as two sets. A ComputedState's two lists are read as sets and its marking as a count per place, because Java builds the lists from a HashSet, so a cached read and a full replay can list the same names in another order (clash evt-c#12, reproduced against the compiled classes), while Rust sorts them and TypeScript keeps insertion order. Ruling D83 (a) promises equal counts and equal sets and leaves the order unspecified; the spec edit of this wave rewords AC3 to say so. Whether the marking map lists a place with no token (a place emptied by TokenRemoved stays listed with an empty list) is not modelled: it counts zero either way.

AC1, reworded by ruling D83 (a) to 'compute_at(events, 0) is the empty state; compute_at(events, len) is the replay of the whole stream', is line 1 at i = 0 and i = len (evt032_zero, evt032_end). The earlier 'matches the final marking shape' compared the replay with the run's final marking, which holds for a stream that reports the initial marking in a MarkingSnapshot right after its ExecutionStarted event, which leaves the replayed state unchanged (Java and TypeScript) and can fail for a Rust or Python stream of a net whose initial marking is not empty: such a stream reports no initial token (no TokenAdded for the initial marking, ruling D76 (a); no MarkingSnapshot producer in Rust), so a TokenRemoved of an initial token does nothing (replay_no_initial; clash evt-c#11). That comparison with a run is the B companion of this ID on the executor event model, wave W11, scoped to Java and TypeScript: there the replayed counts equal the marking on every declared place, and the armed transitions are a subset of the replayed enabled set.

The enabled set is defined by the events (a TransitionEnabled and no TransitionStarted of that transition since) and over-approximates the transitions enabled at that point of the run: a transition whose tokens another firing took, and a reaped transition, stay in it (replay_enabled_overapprox; clash evt-c#10; ruling D83 (a)). The block states the set the replay computes, never the run's enabled set; the subset relation is the W11 companion's.

AC2 (an index beyond the stream length is clamped to the end) is line 1 for an index past the length, since the first i events of a shorter stream are all of it (evt032_clamp). Rust and Python clamp (rust/libpetri-debug/src/marking_cache.rs, target_index.min(events.len()); python/tests/test_marking_cache.py tests it), and so does TypeScript (Array.slice). Java's MarkingCache.computeAt passes the index to subList and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException (clash evt-c#9, reproduced against the compiled classes). Under ruling D83 (a) the line keeps the clamp and Java is a known gap (RD-22 in spec/runtime-defects.md): the spec edit of this wave records it in the implementation status, and evt032_noClampCall, which meets both lines for every index up to the length and answers nothing useful past it, is a mutant of line 1.

AC3, reworded by this wave to 'repeated calls on a stream that only grows at its end return state equal to a from-scratch replay', with a stream that changed otherwise needing invalidate() first, is lines 1 and 2 together: line 1 gives the equality for one call on a coherent cache, line 2 that the cache the call leaves is coherent again, and coherentWith_append that a coherent cache stays coherent when the stream grows at its end, so every call of a sequence on a growing stream that starts from a coherent cache answers the from-scratch replay (evt032_repeated), and after invalidate() (the empty cache, coherent with every stream: coherent_nil) a call answers the replay whatever the stream did before (evt032_after_invalidate). Whether a call reuses a snapshot rather than replaying from the start of the stream (the body's 'replayed from the nearest periodically-cached snapshot rather than from the start of the stream', and AC3's 'Reusing cached snapshots is expected for speed only') is kind Q: the answer is the same and only the time differs, so a cache that never reuses a snapshot meets both lines. The spec edit of this wave says so in the requirement.

Both lines assume the cache is coherent with the stream. The runtime caches are keyed by position only, so a cache filled against a stream that later changed other than by growing at its end (another session's stream, or a debug store that evicted its oldest events and so shifted every index, EVT-024) answers a state that is not the replay (evt032_incoherent) unless invalidate() emptied it first. No debug protocol handler calls invalidate() when its debug store evicts (Java DebugProtocolHandler.computeStateAt over DebugEventStore, which polls its oldest events past capacity; Rust compute_state_at in rust/libpetri-debug/src/debug_protocol_handler.rs; TypeScript computeStateAt; read from the code, not reproduced). The spec edit of this wave records that as a known gap in the implementation status; it is outside this block, which states what the cache answers from a coherent cache.

AC4 (the marking carries token counts; replayed tokens need not carry value payloads) is the granularity of the model: the replayed state holds a count per place and no token, so no line can ask for a payload. The runtimes keep one TokenInfo per token (Java and TypeScript with the event's token data, Rust and Python with none), which the count abstracts.

The snapshot interval is the cache's iv, a parameter of both lines: they hold for every interval, including 0, where no snapshot is ever taken. Its value 256 (SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL in Rust, Java and TypeScript) is configuration, kind N, and the spec does not name it. The runtimes keep no interval in the cache, so a model of a runtime must read the interval from the cache's iv: a model that fixes it at 256 whatever iv says equals the reference on every cache whose iv is 256, the only caches the runtime makes, and still fails both lines on a cache of another interval. A fidelity or B-companion proof therefore models a runtime by its algorithm at iv, not at a constant.

The in-flight transitions are a set of names, as in every runtime, so a transition in flight twice at once (a re-entrant firing, Rust and Python under ruling D8 (b)) leaves the set when its first firing ends (evt032_reentrant; the spec edit of this wave says so). The two lines compare the cache with the replay and hold for every stream; a later line that compares the in-flight set with a run must assume a configuration that is not re-entrant (D8, later line, W11).

Under ruling D20 (clash evt-c#15) the dependency on CONC-025 (the executor's lazily built Marking) is replaced by the events the replay reads: EVT-004, EVT-006 to EVT-012 and EVT-014; EVT-021 stays. The test derivation (a multi-firing run; compute_at at 0, at an intermediate index, at the end and beyond the end; clamping and snapshot reuse) is EVT_032_nonvacuous on the reference with interval 4.

requirements.title: Orchestrator Loop Steps
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (∀ (s0 : XSt N T) (tr : List (XStep N T)),
        XRun R C s0 tr →
          (after Exec001.opensCycle, until isUpdate, never Exec001.isDeadline) tr ∧
            (after Exec001.opensCycle, until Exec001.isDeadline, never isStart) tr ∧
              (after Exec001.beginsCycle, until Exec001.isEndEvents, never isUpdate) tr ∧
                (∀ (i : ℕ),
                    (after Exec001.queuedAtStep1 i, until Exec001.settlesFiring i, never
                        Exec001.passesStep1)
                      tr) ∧
                  (∀ (k : ℕ),
                      (after Exec001.entersStep2With k, until Exec001.dequeuesEvent k,
                          never isUpdate)
                        tr) ∧
                    (∀ (n : String),
                        (after Exec001.reapsName n, until isUpdate, never
                            Exec001.startsName n)
                          tr) ∧
                      (after Exec001.writesMarking C, until isUpdate, never
                          Exec001.isPark)
                        tr) ∧
      on fun s s' ↦ R C s XLbl.update s', shall fun x s' ↦ Exec001.UpdateExact C s'
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C, every run of R under C from any state satisfies lines 1 to 7, and every update step of R under C satisfies line 8:

after each step that begins a cycle (leaves the firing pass or the wait for a running phase that is neither) or deposits tokens outside a firing pass (a commit, a timeout deposit, a publication or an injection taken in a phase other than the firing pass), no deadline step happens before the next enablement update;
after each such step, no start happens before the next deadline step;
after each step that begins a cycle, no enablement update happens before the next end of step 2;

for every firing identity i: after each step that begins a cycle or enters step 1 with i in the completion queue, no publication, injection or start happens before a commit, a fail or a timeout deposit of i;

for every ticket k: after each step that enters step 2 with the event of ticket k in the event queue, no enablement update happens before that event is injected or discarded, or an immediate termination discards the queue;
for every transition name n: after each deadline step that reaps n, no start of n happens before the next enablement update;

after each deposit outside a firing pass, each deposit inside a firing pass that has started a transition, and each start of a transition of the net that has an input or reset arc, no park step happens before the next enablement update;

every update step from s to s' leaves, for every name n and the transition u the net holds under n, u armed or reaped in s' if it is enabled at the marking of s' and the executor is re-entrant or no firing of n is in flight, and n without a stamp if u is not enabled.
quotes: *When* the executor begins a cycle or deposits tokens outside a firing pass, it *shall not* run a deadline step until it has run an enablement update.
*When* the executor begins a cycle or deposits tokens outside a firing pass, it *shall not* start a transition until it has run a deadline step.
*When* the executor begins a cycle, it *shall not* run an enablement update until it has ended step 2.

*When* the executor begins a cycle or enters step 1, it *shall not* deposit a publication, inject an external event or start a transition until it has processed every finished action queued at that moment, whether the action completed, failed or timed out.

*When* the executor enters step 2 of a cycle, it *shall not* run the next enablement update until it has injected or discarded every external event queued at that moment ([ENV-003], [ENV-013], [ENV-015]).
*If* the deadline step of a cycle reaps a transition, *then* the executor *shall not* start that transition before its next enablement update.

*When* the executor starts a transition that has an input or reset arc, or deposits tokens outside a firing pass or inside a firing pass that has started a transition, it *shall not* wait for work until it has run an enablement update.

*When* the executor runs an enablement update, it *shall* leave every transition that is not enabled without a clock, and every enabled transition armed or reaped unless the executor is not re-entrant and a firing of that transition is in flight ([CONC-002]).
assumes: The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. A run (XRun) is a list of consecutive steps (source, label, target) of R, from any state, so every trace line also holds of a run observed from the middle. The labels are the steps of EXEC-001: step 1 settles finished firings (commit, fail, tdeposit) and ends with endCompletions; step 1b deposits mid-action publications (publish, Rust and Python, the markdown sentence 'Between steps 1 and 2'); step 2 injects or discards queued external events (inject, discard) and ends with endEvents; step 3 is update; step 4 is deadline ns, which reaps exactly the names ns; the termination test is finish or begin; step 5 is start, lose and endPass; step 6 is park (the loop blocks) and wake. The loop phase of the state says which step the loop is in, and each phase is entered by the step that ends the one before, so 'enters step 1' is a step whose target is in phase completions and whose source is not, and 'begins a cycle' is a step whose source is the pass or the wait and whose target is a running phase that is neither. The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean), checked rule by rule against the Rust executor.

Every line is a prohibition or, for line 8, a condition on the state an update leaves: nothing here obliges a step to happen. That the loop goes on (the wait wakes on each arrival, a run ends only on its termination test) is CONC-010's and EXEC-040's subject, and a run with no trigger is unconstrained by lines 1 to 7.

Transition names are taken to be pairwise distinct (ruling D10, Cfg.WF.names, which the statement does not assume): lines 6 to 8 work on names, and lines 7 and 8 judge the transition the net holds under the name (findT, the first one with that name). On a net with distinct names this is the transition the start label started; the clock status is kept per name in every runtime.

Ruling D70 (a): the steps run in order, but the wait may itself process the completion, publication or event that ends it (Rust settles, publishes or injects in phase await and then runs step 1), and a synchronous firing may be admitted inside its own pass. The block therefore states the partial order every runtime keeps and no strict order of labels per cycle (R-EXEC-9). The literal acceptance criterion 'No transition fires before completions are processed' is false of Rust read over an admission inside the pass: Rust keeps starting the pass after an inline commit of a synchronous firing (executor_core/executor.rs, the firing loop of Phase 5), the decided run runPass of the design spike. The deposit trigger of lines 1 and 2 reads it 'since the last deposit made outside a firing pass' (design NR-3), which every runtime keeps. A synchronous deposit inside the pass is invisible to the rest of the pass, which is EXEC-003's subject.

The first two EARS sentences are lines 1 and 2: after a cycle begins or a deposit is made outside a pass, a deadline step needs an update first (line 1) and a start needs a deadline step first (line 2), so the update, then the deadline step, then the starts. An executor that skips the update after step 2 and reaps on stale statuses breaks line 1 (EXEC_001_forbids_skipUpdate), and so does one whose wait jumps to the deadline step (EXEC_001_forbids_wakeToDeadline); one whose pass may begin before the deadline step (fire before reap, the run clash013_refresh_rescue of ClashesTime lifts to it) breaks line 2 (EXEC_001_forbids_fireBeforeReap).

The third EARS sentence is line 3: a cycle that begins ends step 2 (endEvents) before its update, so no cycle skips steps 1, 1b and 2. A timer wake that goes straight back to the enablement update (the fast path a Java or TypeScript loop takes if it continues to updateDirtyTransitions when awaitWork returns on its timer, or Rust's Phase 6 timer arm jumping to Phase 3) breaks it (EXEC_001_forbids_wakeToUpdate).

The fourth EARS sentence is line 4, the reading of AC2's first clause and of AC1's first clause: the finished firings queued when a cycle begins or step 1 is entered are processed (committed, failed or their timeout outcome deposited, EXEC-020, EXEC-021, EXEC-022, EXEC-030) before any publication, injection or start, so step 1 comes before steps 1b and 2 and before the pass. The cycle trigger catches an executor that skips step 1; the step 1 trigger one that enters it from elsewhere. A firing that finishes later, while step 1 runs, is a new item; the reference processes it too, as Rust drains its completion channel, but the line does not ask for it. A run that ends step 1 with a firing still queued and then starts a transition breaks the line (EXEC_001_forbids_endWithQueued).

The fifth EARS sentence is line 5, the phase-entry reading of AC3: an event queued when step 2 begins is injected (ENV-003) or, once the executor is closed or stopped, discarded (ENV-013), before the next update. An immediate termination (ENV-015, Java) discards the whole queue at once (the label terminateNow), which releases the line as a discard does. An update that runs with an event still queued breaks the line (EXEC_001_forbids_updateBeforeInject).

The sixth EARS sentence is line 6, the reading of AC4. With the reference ready order a transition that is expired at the cycle reading is not Ready (glossary: Ready, the wording of step 5), so it is not in the order of that pass; the line is what stops a deadline step that only reports the reap and keeps the clock, so that the transition stays armed and an order that tests only the earliest bound would start it in the same cycle: EXEC_001_forbids_reapWithoutDisarm. When a reaped transition may be armed again (only after a write of one of its arc places, ruling D6) is TIME-013's companion line, not this block.

The seventh EARS sentence is line 7, the reading of AC5 and of step 6 under ruling D13 (a): the loop may wait while actions are in flight, but not while a deposit or a consuming start since the last update is unprocessed. Rust runs another cycle after any start and after any dirty bit (fired_any or has_dirty_bits), Java and TypeScript after any dirty bit (hasDirtyBits), and all mark dirty the places a firing consumes from and the places a deposit writes. The start trigger is restricted to transitions with an input or reset arc (a reset arc on an empty place counts, as its start is a write): after a pass whose starts consume nothing, Java and TypeScript may wait at once and Rust runs one more cycle first; no marking, status or event tells the two apart, and both are allowed. A deposit inside a pass counts when the pass has started a transition, which every synchronous deposit inside its own pass does (it follows the start of its firing); the state of an arbitrary executor may hold a firing that is settled inside a pass before any start, and the line does not speak of it. A settle in the wait that goes back to sleep without a new cycle breaks the line (EXEC_001_forbids_parkAfterSettle), and so does a pass that ends in the wait after a synchronous deposit when no transition of the net consumes (the dirty bit of the deposit lost, EXEC_001_forbids_passDepositPark). Which arrivals wake the wait, and that nothing Ready or Expired at the cycle reading may be waited on, are CONC-010's.

The eighth EARS sentence is line 8, the reading of AC6 and of step 3 ('re-evaluate which transitions are enabled based on current marking'): after an update, a transition enabled at the marking is armed or reaped (an update keeps a reaped transition reaped until a write of one of its arc places, ruling D6) unless the executor is not re-entrant and a firing of it is in flight (Cfg.reentrant, ruling D8 (b), CONC-002), and a transition that is not enabled holds no clock. Which stamp an armed transition holds (kept, fresh, or fresh after a restart) is TIME-010's and TIME-012's. An update that re-evaluates nothing, for instance a dirty set cleared before it is read, breaks the line (EXEC_001_forbids_emptyUpdate).

Where the wait sits: no line forbids a park between an update and the end of the next firing pass when nothing was deposited since; CONC-010's park guard (nothing Ready or Expired at the cycle reading, nothing queued) makes such a park indistinguishable from an empty pass followed by the wait.

Ruling D61 (c) and ruling D13 (a), the markdown paragraph on two further points about the cycle: the model takes the update's reading, which stamps what it newly arms, and a reading of its own at the deadline step, never an earlier one (XSt.cyc, atDeadline); the deadline step, the ready order of the pass and the park decision judge at the deadline step's reading. A runtime that takes one reading per cycle (Rust) or a second one after its update that steps 4 and 5 share (TypeScript) is a run of the model; Java's firing pass judges readiness at a third reading of its own, which the ruling does not allow: a recorded executor defect, RD-16 in spec/runtime-defects.md. Those reading lines are TIME-010's companion, TIME-013's companion, TIME-014 line 3 and CONC-010's, and the termination test (finish or begin) made after the update and the deadline step is EXEC-040's and EXEC-041's subject. A terminal place stops the run from any phase (EXEC-042), so a finish may end a cycle anywhere; no line asks for a step after it.

Step 3's clause 'Only transitions affected by token changes need re-evaluation' is a permission, kind Q: the reference re-evaluates every name at the update, the runtimes only the dirty ones, and the dirty scan restores exact enablement (exec001_dirty_set_exact, a citation of updateEnablement_sync); the agreement with RefExec's full re-evaluation is link L9 of ExecLink. The step 3 text cites CONC-005 for the clause (the dirty set), not CONC-004 (the bitmask check). Step 5's ready order is EXEC-002's and TIME-014's; step 1's validation is EXEC-021's; the events each step emits are the EVT blocks'.

AC1 (each cycle runs steps 1 to 5 in order, except as the two exceptions allow) is lines 1 to 4 under ruling D70 (a): queued completions before step 1b, step 2 and the pass (line 4), step 2 ended before the update (line 3), the update before the deadline step (line 1) and the deadline step before any start (line 2), from every cycle that begins. AC2 is line 4 for its first clause and lines 1 and 2 for a deposit made outside a pass. AC3 is line 5, AC4 line 6, AC5 line 7 and AC6 line 8. The test derivation (trace a simple net and check the step order on the event log) is EXEC_001_nonvacuous, five decided reference runs that exercise every trigger and every banned step of the lines, and every release they name: the update, the deadline step, the end of step 2, the commit of a queued firing, the injection, the discard and the immediate termination of a queued event, and the update after a reap followed by the start of the reaped transition.

requirements.title: Priority-Based Firing Order
requirements.statement:
fun O ↦
  ∀ (I : ReadyIn),
    (O I).Perm I.readyList ∧
      List.Pairwise I.tieLt (O I) ∧ (¬I.FastPath → List.Pairwise I.key.lt (O I))
requirements.scope: every executor backend; on the all-immediate fast path only what both outcomes of ruling D14 share
reading: For every input of a pass, fast path included:
the order holds every ready transition exactly once and nothing else;
two transitions of equal priority and equal stamp come in ascending declaration order;
and off the all-immediate fast path, the order is strictly sorted by priority descending, then stamp ascending, then declaration order ascending.
quotes: When multiple transitions are ready to fire (armed, past their earliest bound and not expired; see the glossary), they are sorted by:
Priority, descending: a higher priority fires first.
Stamp, ascending (FIFO): among equal priority, the transition armed first fires first ([TIME-010]).
Declaration order, ascending: among equal priority and equal stamp, the transition declared first fires first.
The ready order of a firing pass *shall* hold every ready transition exactly once and no other transition.
*Where* the net does not take the all-immediate fast path, the ready order *shall* offer a ready transition of higher priority before a ready transition of lower priority.
*Where* the net does not take the all-immediate fast path, the ready order *shall* offer, among ready transitions of equal priority, the one with the earlier stamp first.
The ready order *shall* offer, among ready transitions of equal priority and equal stamp, the earlier-declared one first.
The sort above describes the general path.

Equal priority and equal stamp (transitions newly armed by the enablement update of the same orchestrator cycle share one stamp, [TIME-010]): the tie breaks by ascending declaration order, so the order is fully deterministic.
assumes: The model is an ordering function O from the inputs of one pass (ReadyIn: the net's transitions numbered in declaration order, their priorities, their timings, their stamps and which are ready) to the list of ready transitions in the order the pass offers them for firing. Ready is the glossary term (armed, past the earliest bound, not expired); the stamp is the firing-clock reading taken by the enablement update that most recently newly armed the transition (glossary: Armed, [TIME-010]); the field ReadyIn.clock holds it. In the block these are free inputs; ReadyIn.ofTSt reads them off a timed state of the reference step (the state's stamp, glossary Ready as the ready bit), and ClashesTime shows a bridged input reached by the timed reference step. Which reading becomes a stamp is TIME-010's, not this block's. Which of the offered transitions fires is EXEC-003, not this block.

The four 'shall' sentences are the three lines of the formula. The first is line 1. The fourth, on every input, is line 2. The second and third, off the fast path, are line 3 together with lines 1 and 2: since the order holds every ready transition exactly once, being strictly sorted by the key (priority descending, stamp ascending, declaration order ascending) is the same as offering, of every two ready transitions, the one of higher priority first, of equal priority the one with the earlier stamp first, and of equal priority and stamp the earlier-declared one first (EXEC_002_iff_sentences). The three items of the sort list are the same key, item by item.

'All-immediate fast path': ruling D14 is open. The section names the condition: 'When every transition is `Immediate` and all priorities are equal, backends fire straight from the enablement bitmap in ascending declaration order and do not read the enablement timestamp at all — including when two ready transitions carry different timestamps because one was held across cycles while in flight.' On the fast path the block asks only what both outcomes of D14 share: the first two lines. Whether the fast-path order is declaration order or the general sort when timestamps differ is not encoded; both satisfy the block (EXEC_002_D14_neutral). 'This is deliberate, and every backend takes the path under the same condition.' is part of that paragraph and is not encoded either.

AC1 (priority 10 before priority 5) and AC2 (equal priority on the general path, the one armed first, with the earlier stamp, fires first) are the third line; AC3 (equal priority and equal stamp, ascending declaration order) is the second line, on every input. That transitions newly armed by the enablement update of one cycle share one stamp is TIME-010's stamp rule at the grain of a cycle, deferred to Phase 2 (RefExec); in the block the stamps are free inputs, so AC3 is checked on every pair with equal stamps. EXEC_002_nonvacuous checks the test derivation (priorities 5, 10, 5, all Immediate, armed together), AC2 and AC3 on the reference order, and the fast path.

AC4 (every backend produces the identical ready order) follows on the general path: two ordering functions that satisfy the block agree on every input that does not take the fast path (EXEC_002_unique), because the key is total on distinct transitions. 'Stamp order is the general-path order' is line 3. That the shipped backends compute it is Q evidence, cited from Sched.lean (collect_ready_general_refines) and Refinement.lean (precompiled_refines_bitmap_immediate, the immediate fragment). AC4's 'Backends MUST NOT differ in which order they use, nor in the condition that selects it.' is covered only through the one fixed condition ReadyIn.FastPath, which the block uses for every backend; a backend whose own fast-path condition is narrower or wider is visible only where its order then breaks the first two lines or, off ReadyIn.FastPath, the third (a narrower condition that checks only the ready transitions is killed, EXEC_002_forbids_readyFast). Pinning the fast-path order, which would make every condition disagreement visible, waits for D14.

'Fires first' is read as 'is offered first in the pass's order'; with tokens to compete for, the earlier transition takes them (EXEC-003). That a pass starts its firings in this order is a Phase 2 behaviour line over the executor, not this block.

requirements.title: Priority-Based Firing Order (executor companion)
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  (∀ (C : Cfg N T) (s s' : XSt N T) (tr : List (XStep N T)),
      XRun R C s ((s, XLbl.begin, s') :: tr) →
        (exec002c_starts (exec002c_pass tr)).Sublist
          (List.map (fun x ↦ x.core.name) (readyOrder C s))) ∧
    ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
      on fun s s' ↦ R C s XLbl.update s', shall fun s s' ↦
        ∀ (n m : String) (k k' : ℕ),
          exec002c_fresh s s' n k → exec002c_fresh s s' m k' → k = k'
reading: For every executor R and every configuration C:

in every run of R that opens with a begin step from state s, read up to the end of that pass (the next endPass or begin step), the names of its start steps, in order, are a sublist of the names of the ready order of EXEC-002 at the cycle reading of s (readyOrder C s): the pass starts only transitions of that order, each at most once, in that order;

every update step gives every name it newly arms one and the same stamp: two names that hold, after the step, a stamp they did not hold before it hold the same stamp, a name the step re-stamps with a new value (a restart) included.
quotes: *When* a firing pass starts transitions, the executor *shall* start only transitions of the ready order of that pass, in the order in which that order offers them.
*When* an enablement update newly arms several transitions, a restarted transition included ([TIME-012]), it *shall* give all of them one and the same stamp.

Equal priority and equal stamp (transitions newly armed by the enablement update of the same orchestrator cycle share one stamp, [TIME-010]): the tie breaks by ascending declaration order, so the order is fully deterministic.
assumes: This is the second block of EXEC-002 (ruling D33 (a), design NR-1). The first block, EXEC_002 (EXEC_002.lean), states the ready order as a pure function of one pass's inputs and is unchanged; this block states the two parts that block deferred to the executor model: 'That a pass starts its firings in this order is a Phase 2 behaviour line over the executor' and 'That transitions newly armed by the enablement update of one cycle share one stamp is TIME-010's stamp rule at the grain of a cycle, deferred to Phase 2 (RefExec)'. The block's kind is B, the kind of a behaviour over an executor; the markdown Kind line of EXEC-002 stays F, the kind of its first block, so the two shall sentences this block quotes are behaviour sentences under a section whose Kind line names the first block's kind (recorded for the scribe and the user).

The model is an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean): R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s'. A firing pass opens with a begin step, starts or drops (lose) the transitions of its order one at a time, and ends with an endPass step; 'fire' is read as 'start', as in TIME-014 (a firing starts in the pass and settles later, EXEC-001). Line 1 reads the steps of the pass only, from its begin step to its endPass step (or to the next begin step, for a run whose pass never ends); that no start happens outside a pass is EXEC-003's (a start takes the head of the pass's order). The witness is the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean), which follows the Rust executor.

readyOrder C s is the reference order of EXEC-002 (refReadyOrder, the order the first block's holds theorem checks) over the timed view of s at its cycle reading, the reading the enablement update of the cycle took (R-EXEC-3, ruling D61 (c)); on the all-immediate fast path it is the declaration order (ruling D14 (a)). Line 1 is the first new shall sentence: a pass starts only transitions of that order, and in that order. It adds no constraint beyond other blocks: it is weaker than TIME-014's first line (the names of the start and lose steps are a prefix of the order) together with EXEC-003's first and sixth lines, and follows from them; it is stated here as EXEC-002's own per-ID reading of 'fires first' (ruling D33 (a)). That the pass does not end before it has offered every transition of the order is TIME-014's second line and EXEC-003's, not restated. An executor whose pass offers the ready transitions in descending declaration order (a scan of the enablement bitmap from the top) breaks line 1 (EXEC_002_cycle_forbids_reversedOrder).

Line 2 is the second new shall sentence: one enablement update takes one firing-clock reading and gives it to every transition it newly arms. A restarted transition (TIME-012) counts as newly armed: its stamp changes from the old reading to the new one, which is the glossary entry Armed ('the enablement update that most recently newly armed it') and the sentence's parenthesis. Rust, Java and TypeScript each read the clock once per update (bitmap_backend.rs update_enablement, BitmapNetExecutor.java updateDirtyTransitions, bitmap-net-executor.ts updateDirtyTransitions). Which reading the stamp is, the cycle reading, is TIME-010's companion line, not this block's; this line says only that the stamps are equal, which is what the tie-break of AC3 needs. An executor that reads the clock again for every newly armed transition, so that two transitions armed by one update get different stamps, breaks it (EXEC_002_cycle_forbids_staggered).

The three sentences of the sort list and the four shall sentences of the first block are the first block's subject, at the grain of one pass's inputs; with line 1 they apply to the starts of a pass. AC1 (priority 10 before priority 5) and AC2 (equal priority, the earlier stamp first) are the first block's third line, applied to the starts of the pass by line 1. AC3 (equal priority and equal stamp, ascending declaration order) is the first block's second line for the order, line 2 for 'share one stamp', and line 1 for 'fires': EXEC_002_cycle_nonvacuous shows four transitions of one priority armed by one update at stamp 0 and started in declaration order. AC4 (every backend produces the identical ready order) is the first block's, cited from Sched.lean and Refinement.lean; both backends are runs of RefExec (CONC-020, a later block).

The test derivation (priorities 5, 10, 5, enabled together, fired P10 then P5 then P5) is the first block's example applied to the starts of a pass by line 1. The decided runs here take the all-immediate path, because the kernel does not evaluate the general path's merge sort on two or more ready transitions (as in EXEC-003 and TIME-014); line 1 reads the order through readyOrder whatever path the net takes.

requirements.title: Competitive Conflict Resolution
requirements.statement:
fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R ↦
  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),
    (∀ (n : String) (sy : Bool),
        on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.start n sy) s', shall fun s s' ↦
          ∃ t rest,
            s.order = t :: rest ∧
              t.core.name = n ∧
                (stampOf (s.st n)).isSome = true ∧
                  Novel.Seam.enabledNA (qCount (vis s)) t.core = true ∧ s'.order = rest) ∧
      (∀ (n : String) (sy : Bool),
          on fun s s' ↦ R C s (XLbl.start n sy) s', shall fun s s' ↦
            ∃ t rest,
              s.order = t :: rest ∧
